messages.content:
## File Read Hotness Analysis

### Key Finding: No Hot-Spot Concentration
Across all 200 visible results (the full result set is truncated beyond 200 rows), **every single file has a read_count of exactly 1**. There are no repeatedly-read "hot" files in this dataset — each file was read from disk precisely once during the simulation. All files also show **distinct_sites = 1** and **distinct_hosts = 1**, meaning each read involved a single site and single host.

### File Characteristics
All files follow the `lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_*.fits` naming convention. File sizes within the visible results range from approximately **65.8 MB** (`lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_98_0002.fits`, 65,788,748 bytes) to **133.1 MB** (`lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_96_0001.fits`, 133,105,176 bytes).

### Read Performance: Consistent ~10 GB/s Throughput
The dominant pattern is an average effective read throughput of approximately **10 GB/s** across nearly all files, with very short read durations (roughly 8–18 milliseconds). This suggests reads are served from a fast local storage tier.

### Notable Outlier
One file stands out: **`lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_960_0000.fits`** achieved only **5.0 GB/s** effective throughput with an avg_read_duration of **0.01827 seconds** — roughly double the typical duration for a similarly-sized file. This halved throughput suggests it was read under constrained disk bandwidth (e.g., disk contention or a slower storage device).

### Operational Takeaway
Since every file is read at most once, there is no data reuse occurring — no caching benefit is being realized. If any file were read multiple times, it would stand out immediately; the uniform read_count=1 pattern suggests either a single-pass workflow or that caching/reuse was not modeled.

messages.content:
## Site-by-Site Inbound vs. Outbound Transfer Analysis

### Sites With Both Directions (Directional Comparison Possible)

**Base**
- Counts are nearly balanced: 505 inbound vs. 509 outbound transfers.
- Inbound carries smaller average files (~84.1 MB) than outbound (~100.2 MB).
- Provisioned bandwidth is higher inbound (12,500 MB/s) than outbound (~9,914 MB/s).
- Link load is substantially higher inbound (~10,578 MB/s) vs. outbound (~4,949 MB/s).
- **Effective throughput is roughly 2× higher inbound (~29.9 MB/s) than outbound (~14.6 MB/s).** Base shows a clear inbound advantage — outbound links appear more congested relative to their load.

**USDF**
- Volume is heavily skewed: 2,676 outbound vs. only 445 inbound transfers.
- Inbound provisioned bandwidth is far higher (~12,500 MB/s) than outbound (~2,032 MB/s).
- Link load follows the same pattern: inbound ~5,639 MB/s vs. outbound ~1,648 MB/s.
- **Effective throughput is ~7.8× higher inbound (~16.3 MB/s) than outbound (~2.1 MB/s).** USDF is a strong net sender with a heavily constrained outbound pipe — a textbook directional bottleneck on egress.

---

### Sites With Only One Direction (No Comparison Possible)

| Site | Direction | Transfers | Avg File Size | Provisioned BW | Link Load | Effective Throughput |
|------|-----------|-----------|---------------|----------------|-----------|----------------------|
| FrDF | inbound only | 1,846 | ~92.0 MB | ~1,250 MB/s | ~1,189 MB/s | ~1.1 MB/s |
| UKDF | inbound only | 784 | ~88.8 MB | ~1,250 MB/s | ~1,116 MB/s | ~2.3 MB/s |
| Summit | outbound only | 395 | ~79.7 MB | ~11,845 MB/s | ~10,109 MB/s | ~33.5 MB/s |

- **FrDF and UKDF** receive data exclusively (no outbound records), both on narrow 1,250 MB/s provisioned links with low effective throughputs (~1.1 and ~2.3 MB/s). Their high link-load-to-bandwidth ratios (~95% and ~89%) indicate near-saturated inbound links.
- **Summit** only sends data, on a high-capacity ~11,845 MB/s link running at ~85% load with the highest effective throughput in the dataset (~33.5 MB/s).

---

### Summary of Asymmetries

| Site | Asymmetry Type | Key Signal |
|------|----------------|------------|
| Base | Inbound favored | Inbound throughput 2× outbound despite near-equal transfer counts |
| USDF | Egress bottleneck | Outbound throughput 7.8× lower; 6× more outbound transfers on narrow bandwidth |
| FrDF | Inbound-only, link near-saturated | ~95% link load, very low effective throughput |
| UKDF | Inbound-only, link near-saturated | ~89% link load, low effective throughput |
| Summit | Outbound-only, high performance | Highest effective throughput; no inbound data |

messages.content:
## File Write Performance by Site and Size Bucket

### Overview
The results cover 12 site/bucket combinations across 4 sites (Base, FrDF, UKDF, USDF) and 3 size classes. All metrics are from completed writes (STATE='Finished'). Bandwidth figures use GB/s throughout.

---

### Summary Table

| Site | Bucket | Count | Avg Duration (s) | Disk Write BW | Avg Effective Throughput | Total Written |
|------|--------|------:|------------------:|--------------:|------------------------:|-------------:|
| Base | Small | 510 | 0.113 | 5.00 GB/s | 0.91 GB/s | 24.0 GB |
| Base | Medium | 26 | 0.130 | 5.00 GB/s | 2.25 GB/s | 6.56 GB |
| Base | Large | 3 | 0.364 | 5.00 GB/s | 3.21 GB/s | 3.13 GB |
| FrDF | Small | 132 | 0.012 | 10.00 GB/s | 5.12 GB/s | 7.30 GB |
| FrDF | Medium | 133 | 0.131 | 10.00 GB/s | 4.33 GB/s | 55.8 GB |
| FrDF | Large | 14 | 0.239 | 10.00 GB/s | 6.59 GB/s | 20.3 GB |
| UKDF | Small | 98 | 0.012 | 10.00 GB/s | 4.69 GB/s | 5.11 GB |
| UKDF | Medium | 56 | 0.099 | 10.00 GB/s | 5.13 GB/s | 20.4 GB |
| UKDF | Large | 6 | 0.197 | 10.00 GB/s | 8.22 GB/s | 9.44 GB |
| USDF | Small | 438 | 0.034 | 10.00 GB/s | 3.35 GB/s | 24.6 GB |
| USDF | Medium | 376 | 0.119 | 10.00 GB/s | 4.22 GB/s | 116.5 GB |
| USDF | Large | 24 | 0.311 | 10.00 GB/s | 5.84 GB/s | 37.0 GB |

---

### Key Findings

**1. Base is the constrained site.**
Base has a configured disk write bandwidth of 5.00 GB/s — half that of FrDF, UKDF, and USDF (all 10.00 GB/s). Its small-file effective throughput (0.91 GB/s) is the lowest in the entire dataset, roughly 5–6× below comparable sites.

**2. File size consistently increases effective throughput at all sites.**
Across every site, larger files achieve higher effective throughput than smaller ones (e.g., at UKDF: small=4.69 GB/s → medium=5.13 GB/s → large=8.22 GB/s). Large files at UKDF reach 8.22 GB/s, the highest observed — approaching the 10 GB/s ceiling.

**3. Effective throughput is always below the configured disk BW**, indicating overhead (latency, scheduling, fragmentation). At Base, the gap is most severe for small files: the effective 0.91 GB/s is only ~18% of the 5.00 GB/s disk bandwidth. At FrDF/UKDF/USDF, large files recover to 66–82% efficiency.

**4. Write durations increase with file size, but not proportionally.**
Large files take ~0.20–0.36 s vs. ~0.01–0.11 s for small files, confirming that larger writes achieve better per-byte efficiency even though absolute time is higher.

**5. USDF handles the highest total write volume.**
USDF's medium bucket alone accounts for 116.5 GB across 376 writes, far exceeding any other single bucket. USDF also leads in large-file count (24 writes, 37.0 GB).

**6. Small-file write volume is dominated by Base (510 writes, 24.0 GB) and USDF (438 writes, 24.6 GB)**, suggesting these two sites process the most small-file I/O workloads.

messages.content:
## Job Queue Time Breakdown by Site

### Key Finding: File Staging is the Sole Source of Queue Delay — Resource Contention is Zero Everywhere

Across all four sites, **resource-waiting queue time is exactly 0.0** (both average and maximum). Every second of queuing delay comes entirely from **file-transfer staging**.

---

### Site-by-Site Summary

| Site | Jobs | Avg File-Transfer Queue (s) | Max File-Transfer Queue (s) | Avg Resource-Wait (s) | Avg Total Queue (s) |
|------|------|----------------------------|----------------------------|----------------------|---------------------|
| **FrDF** | 138 | 87.52 | 144.16 | 0.0 | 87.52 |
| **UKDF** | 80 | 33.75 | 58.90 | 0.0 | 33.75 |
| **Base** | 344 | 2.14 | 8.60 | 0.0 | 2.14 |
| **USDF** | 438 | −0.21 | 8.57 | 0.0 | −0.21 |

---

### Operational Takeaways

1. **FrDF is the worst-affected site**: average file-transfer queue time of **87.52 s** and a peak of **144.16 s** — roughly 2.6× worse than UKDF and ~41× worse than Base. File staging is a significant bottleneck here.

2. **UKDF is a moderate concern**: average of **33.75 s** and peak of **58.90 s** — elevated but far below FrDF.

3. **Base and USDF are largely unaffected**: averages of **2.14 s** and **−0.21 s** respectively. The slightly negative average at USDF (largest site at 438 jobs) is a simulation artefact and operationally negligible.

4. **Resource contention is a non-issue grid-wide**: no site shows any resource-waiting queue time, meaning compute slots are always available when jobs are ready to run. Investment in alleviating queuing should target **network bandwidth or file pre-staging to FrDF and UKDF**, not CPU provisioning.

messages.content:
## File Transfer Performance by Network Latency Bucket

Three latency buckets are present in the data (no transfers recorded with latency below 1 ms).

| Metric | Low (1–10 ms) | Medium (10–100 ms) | High (≥100 ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Transfer count** | 319 | 631 | 2,630 |
| **Avg file size** | 80.0 MB | 95.6 MB | 91.0 MB |
| **Avg duration** | 2.09 s | 5.86 s | 93.51 s |
| **Avg effective throughput** | 38.2 MB/s | 16.2 MB/s | 1.5 MB/s |
| **Avg link load** | 12,407.6 MB/s | 6,170.5 MB/s | 1,167.1 MB/s |
| **Avg provisioned bandwidth** | 12,500 MB/s | 12,500 MB/s | 1,250 MB/s |

### Key Observations

1. **Latency dominates throughput degradation.** Moving from low to high latency, average effective throughput collapses from 38.2 MB/s → 16.2 MB/s → 1.5 MB/s — a **25× drop** between the best and worst buckets — despite file sizes being broadly similar (~80–96 MB across all buckets).

2. **High-latency links also carry lower provisioned bandwidth** (1,250 MB/s vs. 12,500 MB/s for the other two buckets), compounding the performance penalty. The vast majority of transfers (2,630 of 3,580) operate on these constrained links.

3. **Link utilisation reflects congestion.** Low-latency links show average load of 12,407.6 MB/s against a 12,500 MB/s provisioned capacity (~99% utilised), whereas high-latency links run at ~1,167 MB/s against 1,250 MB/s (~93% utilised) — all buckets operate near saturation, meaning latency, not spare capacity, is the primary constraint.

4. **Duration impact is severe at high latency**: average transfer time of 93.51 s on high-latency links vs. 2.09 s on low-latency links represents a **45× slowdown**, making these links a critical bottleneck for grid workflow completion times.

messages.content:
## Inbound File Transfer Distribution by Destination Site

Four destination sites received completed transfers, ranked by total bytes received:

| Site | Transfers | Total Received | Avg File Size | Min File Size | Max File Size | Avg Link Load | Avg Duration |
|------|-----------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|--------------|
| **FrDF** | 1,846 | 169.9 GB | 92.0 MB | 26.9 MB | 189.1 MB | 1.19 B/s (×10⁹) | 114.7 s |
| **UKDF** | 784 | 69.6 GB | 88.8 MB | 25.6 MB | 182.0 MB | 1.12 B/s (×10⁹) | 43.6 s |
| **USDF** | 445 | 43.4 GB | 97.5 MB | 52.6 MB | 153.8 MB | 5.64 B/s (×10⁹) | 5.9 s |
| **Base** | 505 | 42.5 GB | 84.1 MB | 32.7 MB | 170.2 MB | 10.58 B/s (×10⁹) | 3.4 s |

### Key Takeaways

- **FrDF is the dominant data consumer** by a wide margin — it received 169.9 GB across 1,846 transfers, more than double the next site (UKDF at 69.6 GB) and roughly 4× USDF or Base.
- **File size profiles are broadly similar** across all sites (averages range from 84–98 MB), meaning FrDF's data dominance comes from **transfer volume**, not from receiving unusually large files.
- **USDF and Base complete transfers far faster** despite similar data volumes to each other — average durations of 5.9 s and 3.4 s respectively, compared to 43.6 s (UKDF) and 114.7 s (FrDF). Their dramatically higher average link loads (5.6×10⁹ and 10.6×10⁹ vs. ~1.1×10⁹ for FrDF/UKDF) confirm they benefit from much higher-bandwidth connections.
- **FrDF's long average duration (114.7 s)** paired with the lowest link load suggests it operates on a constrained network path, making it a potential bottleneck despite being the largest consumer.

messages.content:
## Disk Write Throughput vs. Provisioned Capacity by Site

Across all four sites, no site reaches even 50% of its provisioned disk write bandwidth, indicating consistently underutilized write capacity grid-wide.

### Site-by-Site Breakdown (ordered by utilization, lowest first)

| Site | Writes | Avg Effective BW | Avg Provisioned BW | Avg Utilization | Total Written |
|------|--------|------------------|--------------------|-----------------|---------------|
| **Base** | 539 | ~0.99 GB/s | 5.0 GB/s | **19.8%** | ~33.7 GB |
| **USDF** | 838 | ~3.81 GB/s | 10.0 GB/s | **38.1%** | ~178.1 GB |
| **FrDF** | 279 | ~4.82 GB/s | 10.0 GB/s | **48.2%** | ~83.5 GB |
| **UKDF** | 160 | ~4.98 GB/s | 10.0 GB/s | **49.8%** | ~35.0 GB |

### Key Observations

- **Base is the most concerning outlier**: its provisioned bandwidth is 5.0 GB/s, but actual effective throughput averages only ~0.99 GB/s — just **19.8% utilization**. This is the largest gap in both absolute and relative terms, and Base also has a lower provisioned capacity than the other three sites.
- **USDF** handles by far the most write volume (~178.1 GB across 838 writes) yet achieves only 38.1% utilization of its 10.0 GB/s provision.
- **FrDF and UKDF** are closest to capacity (48.2% and 49.8%, respectively), but still leave roughly half their provisioned write bandwidth unused.
- The three 10.0 GB/s sites (USDF, FrDF, UKDF) show a clear pattern: more write operations correlate with *lower* utilization, suggesting contention or I/O scheduling overhead rather than bandwidth saturation.

**Bottom line**: Base warrants immediate investigation — its effective write throughput falls ~80% short of provisioned capacity, far beyond the ~50% shortfall seen at the other sites.

## File Transfer Activity Summary

### Key Structural Finding
Across all 200 rows returned (results are truncated, so more files exist), **every file was transferred exactly once**, always between a single source and a single destination site. There is no file with repeat transfers, multi-source replication, or fan-out distribution visible in these results.

### Most Actively Migrated Files (by Volume)
The top 25 rows visible span a narrow size band:

| Rank | File | Total Bytes | Avg Duration (s) | Avg Throughput (B/s) |
|------|------|------------|-----------------|---------------------|
| 1 | lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_420_0002.fits | 189,147,285 | 16.96 | 11,153,403 |
| 2 | lsst_Coadd_938_0034.fits | 185,362,334 | 144.61 | 1,281,789 |
| 3 | lsst_Coadd_573_0021.fits | 182,040,744 | 59.16 | 3,076,890 |

The 200th visible entry (lsst_Coadd_256_0010.fits) sits at **155,125,870 bytes**, indicating the displayed results cover a relatively tight size range (~155–189 MB per file).

### Two Distinct Transfer Performance Tiers
Three duration clusters are evident in the data:

- **Fast (~8–17 s):** e.g., lsst_Coadd_883_0023.fits (9.35 s) and lsst_Coadd_883_0021.fits (8.68 s) achieve throughputs of **18.2 MB/s and 18.0 MB/s** respectively — the highest in the visible results.
- **Medium (~57–60 s):** Files like the lsst_Coadd_573_* series achieve ~3.0–2.7 MB/s.
- **Slow (~142–145 s):** A large cluster of Coadd and DiffImaging files (e.g., lsst_Coadd_938_0034.fits at 144.6 s) achieve only ~1.1–1.3 MB/s — the lowest throughput tier visible.

### File Type Distribution (in visible 200 rows)
The transferred files are predominantly **Coadd** products, with at least one **SingleFrame_Cal** (the top entry) and one **DiffImaging** file (lsst_DiffImaging_676_0000.fits at rank 12, 162,945,430 bytes, 143.2 s, ~1.14 MB/s).

### Operational Takeaway
No file is being repeatedly transferred or distributed to multiple sites — each object moves once, point-to-point. The dominant performance differentiator is **which network path is used**: the slow-tier transfers (≥142 s) carry comparably sized files as the fast-tier but at **~14–17× lower throughput**, pointing to bandwidth or congestion differences on specific links rather than file size as the bottleneck.

messages.content:
## Queuing Analysis: CPU Congestion vs. File Staging

### Key Finding: Resource Waiting is Zero Everywhere

Across all 5 site/bucket combinations, **avg_resource_waiting_queue_time = 0.0** and **max_resource_waiting_queue_time = 0.0**. CPU congestion contributes **nothing** to queuing. File staging (file-transfer queue time) is the **sole queuing driver** in every case, and total queue time equals file-transfer queue time exactly.

---

### Site-by-Site Breakdown

| Site | CPU Bucket | Jobs | Avg File-Transfer Queue (s) | Avg Total Queue (s) |
|------|-----------|------|-----------------------------|---------------------|
| Base | low (<0.3) | 171 | 2.44 | 2.44 |
| Base | medium (0.3–0.7) | 173 | 1.84 | 1.84 |
| FrDF | low (<0.3) | 138 | **87.52** | 87.52 |
| UKDF | low (<0.3) | 80 | 33.75 | 33.75 |
| USDF | low (<0.3) | 438 | −0.21 *(artifact)* | −0.21 |

---

### Operational Takeaways

1. **No high CPU utilization bucket appears anywhere** — the simulation never reached ≥0.7 site CPU utilization for completed jobs.
2. **FrDF is the worst performer**: 87.52 s average file-transfer queue time on 138 jobs, the highest in the dataset — despite low CPU load, file staging is severely bottlenecked.
3. **UKDF is second worst**: 33.75 s on 80 jobs, also under low CPU load.
4. **Base shows an inverse CPU–queue relationship**: medium-CPU jobs (173) have a *lower* file-transfer queue (1.84 s) than low-CPU jobs (2.44 s), suggesting no harmful interaction between CPU load and file staging at this site.
5. **USDF's −0.21 s** is a simulation rounding artifact on 438 jobs and is effectively zero queue time — the best-performing site by far.
6. **Intervention priority**: Target FrDF's file-transfer infrastructure first, then UKDF's. CPU scheduling is not a concern at any site in this simulation.

messages.content:
## Key Finding: No Grid CPU Congestion Observed

All 1,000 jobs across all four sites fall exclusively into the **low (<0.3)** grid CPU utilization bucket at execution start. The medium (0.3–0.7) and high (≥0.7) buckets are entirely empty, meaning the simulation never experienced meaningful grid-level CPU saturation at the moment jobs began — making a cross-bucket congestion comparison impossible from this dataset.

---

### Per-Site Summary (Low Grid CPU Utilization Only)

| Site | Jobs | Avg Duration | Avg Flops | Avg Effective Flop Rate | Avg Site CPU Util at Start |
|------|------|-------------|-----------|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Base | 344 | 1.53 × 10⁻⁷ | 1,899 | 4.23 × 10⁹ | 0.302 |
| FrDF | 138 | 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ | 34,540 | 1.82 × 10¹⁰ | 0.097 |
| UKDF | 80 | 1.13 × 10⁻⁶ | 25,902 | 1.66 × 10¹⁰ | 0.130 |
| USDF | 438 | 1.01 × 10⁻⁶ | 22,138 | 1.53 × 10¹⁰ | 0.096 |

---

### Operational Takeaways

1. **Grid saturation never occurred** at job-start time — the original question about whether grid-level congestion degrades throughput cannot be answered from this simulation run.
2. **Site-level variation is substantial** even without grid congestion: Base jobs carry ~16× fewer flops than FrDF jobs and achieve a correspondingly lower effective flop rate (4.23 × 10⁹ vs. 1.82 × 10¹⁰), suggesting Base handles much lighter workloads.
3. **Base** is the only site where site CPU utilization at start (0.302) approaches the medium threshold, yet it handles the most jobs (344) — indicating local pressure independent of grid-wide utilization.
4. To study congestion effects, the simulation would need to be rerun under higher grid load conditions.

## Disk Read Bandwidth Utilization by Site

Four sites are captured across **6,836 total completed file reads**, revealing a stark two-tier split in how effectively sites use their provisioned disk capacity.

### High-Utilization Sites (Near Saturation)
| Site | Reads | Avg File Size | Avg Throughput | Provisioned BW | Utilization |
|------|-------|--------------|----------------|----------------|-------------|
| **FrDF** | 1,846 | 92.0 MB | 9.84 GB/s | 10.0 GB/s | **98.4%** |

messages.content:
## Inter-Site File Transfer Congestion Analysis

Across **10 unique source-to-destination routes**, three stand out as severely congested — their average link loads are an order of magnitude higher than the rest.

---

### Top-3 Most Congested Routes (Near Saturation)

| Route | Transfers | Total Transferred | Avg File Size | Avg Duration (s) | Avg Throughput | Avg Link Load | Max Link Load |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Summit → Base** | 319 | 25.5 GB | ~80.0 MB | 2.09 s | ~38.2 MB/s | **~12.4 GB/s** | ~12.5 GB/s |
| **USDF → Base** | 186 | 17.0 GB | ~91.1 MB | 5.66 s | ~15.8 MB/s | **~7.4 GB/s** | ~12.5 GB/s |
| **Base → USDF** | 392 | 39.2 GB | ~100.0 MB | 6.07 s | ~16.4 MB/s | **~6.3 GB/s** | ~12.5 GB/s |

All three routes have a maximum link load of essentially **12.5 GB/s**, indicating they repeatedly hit what appears to be a hard network capacity ceiling. Summit → Base is the single most congested route on average.

---

### Remaining 7 Routes (Lower Congestion)

| Route | Transfers | Avg Link Load | Max Link Load |
|---|---|---|---|
| USDF → FrDF | 1,770 | ~1.22 GB/s | ~1.25 GB/s |
| USDF → UKDF | 720 | ~1.19 GB/s | ~1.25 GB/s |
| Summit → USDF | 53 | ~619 MB/s | ~1.22 GB/s |
| Base → FrDF | 61 | ~427 MB/s | ~840 MB/s |
| Base → UKDF | 56 | ~292 MB/s | ~574 MB/s |
| Summit → FrDF | 15 | ~109 MB/s | ~205 MB/s |
| Summit → UKDF | 8 | ~46 MB/s | ~82 MB/s |

---

### Key Operational Takeaways

1. **The Base site is the congestion bottleneck.** Three of the four most loaded routes terminate at or originate from Base, with Summit → Base being the worst.
2. **USDF ↔ FrDF is the highest-volume corridor** (1,770 transfers, 162.3 GB total), but with a much lower average link load (~1.22 GB/s), suggesting it is well-provisioned relative to demand.
3. **Summit-originated transfers are fast but saturating** — Summit → Base averages only 2.09 s per file yet still drives the highest average link load, pointing to a very high-bandwidth but fully utilized link.
4. **Summit → UKDF** is the least loaded route (avg ~46 MB/s, only 8 transfers), representing the most underutilized path in the simulation.

## File-Transfer Queue Time vs. Job Retry & Performance Analysis

### Summary Table

| Bucket | Jobs | Avg Retries | Retry Rate | Avg Exec Duration (s) | Avg Cost | Avg Total I/O Read Time (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| None (= 0 s) | 7 | 0.0 | 0.0% | 3.89 × 10⁻⁷ | −1.0 | 0.051 |

| Medium (60–300 s) | 90 | 0.0 | 0.0% | 2.06 × 10⁻⁶ | −1.0 | 0.191 |
| Long (≥ 300 s) | — | — | — | — | — | — |

### Key Findings

1. **No retries or failures observed anywhere.** All three buckets show avg_retries = 0.0 and retry_rate = 0.0%. There is no evidence in this dataset that longer file-staging queues are associated with higher retry rates — because retry rates are uniformly zero.

2. **No long-queue jobs exist.** The ≥300 s bucket produced no rows, meaning no completed job executions experienced a file-transfer queue time of 300 s or more.

3. **Execution durations are negligibly small** across all buckets (sub-microsecond), suggesting these may represent very lightweight or synthetic workloads.

4. **Average cost is −1.0 for all buckets**, which is a sentinel/placeholder value indicating cost was not tracked or is undefined for these jobs.

The data provides **no support** for the hypothesis that longer file-staging queues drive higher job failure or retry rates; the retry signal is entirely absent. The dominant workload sits in the short-queue bucket (903 of 1,000 total jobs, or 90.3%).

## 20 Most Severely Delayed Completed Job Executions

### Headline Pattern
All 20 of the most-delayed jobs share the same profile: **site FrDF**, **status "finished"**, **0 retries**, and **cost –1.0** (indicating cost is not tracked or not applicable at this site). The delay is entirely driven by file-transfer queue time — resource-waiting queue time is **0.0 for every single job**.

---

### Top 5 Most Delayed Jobs

| Rank | Job ID | Host | Total Queue Time (s) | File-Transfer Queue (s) | Resource-Wait Queue (s) | Exec Duration (s) |
|------|--------|------|---------------------:|------------------------:|------------------------:|------------------:|
| 1 | 938 | FrDF_cpu-1 | 144.156 | 144.156 | 0.0 | ~6.1 × 10⁻⁶ |
| 2 | 903 | FrDF_cpu-10 | 143.407 | 143.407 | 0.0 | ~3.4 × 10⁻⁶ |
| 3 | 259 | FrDF_cpu-117 | 143.180 | 143.180 | 0.0 | ~3.1 × 10⁻⁶ |
| 4 | 676 | FrDF_cpu-105 | 143.161 | 143.161 | 0.0 | ~5.3 × 10⁻⁷ |
| 5 | 946 | FrDF_cpu-1 | 142.785 | 142.785 | 0.0 | ~3.2 × 10⁻⁶ |

---

### Key Findings

1. **File-transfer queue time is the sole bottleneck.** Across all 20 jobs, `total_queue_time = file_transfer_queue_time` exactly — resource-waiting contributes nothing. This points squarely at **network or storage I/O saturation at FrDF**, not CPU slot availability.

2. **Delay range is narrow (141.94 s – 144.16 s).** The 20th job (Job 66, FrDF_cpu-119, 141.943 s) is only ~2.2 seconds less delayed than the worst offender, suggesting a systemic, site-wide condition rather than isolated incidents.

3. **Execution itself is negligible.** All actual compute durations are on the order of microseconds (< 7 × 10⁻⁶ s), meaning jobs spend effectively **100% of their elapsed time waiting for file transfers** — the compute work is trivial once started.

4. **No retries.** All 20 jobs completed on the first attempt (retries = 0), so the delay is not caused by job failures forcing re-queuing.

5. **FrDF is the exclusive site.** Every one of the 20 most-delayed jobs ran at FrDF, across 13 distinct hosts (FrDF_cpu-0 through FrDF_cpu-119). This is a **site-level, not host-level, issue**.

### Operational Recommendation
Investigate FrDF's file-transfer infrastructure — specifically its inbound/outbound network bandwidth, storage throughput, and transfer queue management — as it is the singular root cause of these ~142–144 second scheduling delays for all 20 flagged jobs.

## Key Findings

### Site-by-Site Summary (No-Retry Jobs Only)

| Site | Job Count | Avg Speed (GFlops/s) | Avg Flops | Avg Cores | Avg Duration (s) |

| FrDF | 138 | 3.2 | 34,540 | 5.67 | 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ |
| UKDF | 80 | 3.2 | 25,902 | 5.20 | 1.13 × 10⁻⁶ |
| USDF | 438 | 3.2 | 22,138 | 4.79 | 1.01 × 10⁻⁶ |

### Access Distribution
Every one of the 25 visible rows (out of 200 returned, results truncated) shows an identical split: **1 local read and 1 network transfer** per file, giving each a combined access count of 2. | Duration range | 0.0066 s – 0.0133 s | 5.32 s – 10.44 s |

**Resource scarcity is not a bottleneck anywhere.** Optimization effort should target file-staging pipelines, prioritizing FrDF (87.52 s average delay) and UKDF (33.75 s) — improving pre-staging, caching, or network bandwidth to those sites would yield the largest scheduling gains.

messages.content:
## Average and Maximum Job Execution Duration by Site

All durations are in **microseconds (µs)**. Four sites are covered, ordered by average duration descending:

| Site | Jobs | Avg Duration (µs) | Max Duration (µs) |
|------|------|--------------------|-------------------|
| **FrDF** | 144 | 1.548 | 6.163 |
| **UKDF** | 72 | 1.328 | 5.040 |
| **USDF** | 434 | 1.028 | 7.439 |
| **Base** | 350 | 0.147 | 4.381 |

### Key Observations

- **FrDF** has the slowest average job execution at ~1.55 µs, despite processing only 144 jobs — the second-lowest volume.
- **UKDF** is second slowest (~1.33 µs avg) and has the fewest jobs (72).
- **USDF** handles the highest volume (434 jobs) yet posts the highest single-job peak at **7.44 µs** — the longest individual execution across all sites — while maintaining a moderate average of ~1.03 µs.
- **Base** is by far the fastest on average (~0.15 µs), roughly **10× faster** than FrDF, despite running 350 jobs. Its max (~4.38 µs) is also the lowest across all sites.

### Summary
Base site is the most consistently fast executor. USDF carries the largest workload but exhibits the widest performance spread (low average, highest peak). FrDF and UKDF run fewer jobs but at higher average durations.

**All 10 transfers occurred on the same route: USDF → FrDF**, with durations ranging from **161.38 s to 163.10 s** — a very narrow band of roughly 1.7 seconds separating first from last.

| Rank | Job | File | Size (MB) | Duration (s) |

| 3 | 314 | lsst_Coadd_314_0002.fits | 186.9 | 162.94 |
| 4 | 179 | lsst_Coadd_179_0038.fits | 175.6 | 162.23 |
| 5 | 560 | lsst_Coadd_560_0031.fits | 170.2 | 161.88 |
| 6 | 423 | lsst_Coadd_423_0005.fits | 166.6 | 161.64 |
| 7 | 293 | lsst_Coadd_293_0021.fits | 165.9 | 161.60 |
| 8 | 298 | lsst_DiffImaging_298_0001.fits | 165.8 | 161.60 |
| 9 | 182 | lsst_Coadd_182_0023.fits | 163.4 | 161.44 |
| 10 | 959 | lsst_Coadd_959_0022.fits | 162.4 | 161.38 |

## Grid-Wide CPU Utilization Over Time

The query results cover **only a single 1-hour bucket** (hour 0), meaning all 1,000 job execution starts occurred within the first hour of the simulation.

| Hour Bucket | Avg Grid CPU Util | Peak Grid CPU Util | Execution Starts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | ~2.45 × 10⁻¹³ | ~4.73 × 10⁻¹³ | 1,000 |

### Key Observations

- **Effectively zero CPU utilization**: Both the average (~2.45 × 10⁻¹³) and peak (~4.73 × 10⁻¹³) grid CPU utilization are essentially zero at the moment jobs *start*. This is consistent with the fact that these are **start-of-execution** snapshots — the jobs have just been dispatched and have not yet consumed meaningful CPU cycles on the grid.
- **No temporal evolution visible**: There is only one time bucket, so no trend or ramp-up pattern can be observed across hours.
- **All activity is concentrated in hour 0**: All 1,000 job execution starts fall within the first 3,600 simulation-time units.

### Operational Takeaway
The near-zero CPU utilization at job start suggests the grid begins the simulation largely idle and jobs are launched in a burst at the very beginning. To observe how utilization *evolves*, monitoring utilization at job **completion** events (or sampling at finer granularity across a longer simulation run) would provide more meaningful trend data.

## Site-Level Storage Utilization at Job Allocation Completion

Across **4 sites** and a total of **1,000 completed job allocations**, storage utilization at allocation finish time is uniformly very low — well below 0.03% at every site.

| Site | Allocations | Avg Storage Util | Peak Storage Util |
|------|-------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| **Base** | 350 | 0.0002680 (≈0.027%) | 0.0002680 (≈0.027%) |
| **USDF** | 434 | 0.0001118 (≈0.011%) | 0.0001118 (≈0.011%) |
| **UKDF** | 72 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| **FrDF** | 144 | 0.0 | 0.0 |

### Key Observations

1. **Base** has the highest utilization, but its peak and average are identical (≈0.027%), meaning storage utilization was **flat across all 350 allocations** — no variance observed.
2. **USDF** is similar: peak equals average (≈0.011%) across all 434 allocations, again indicating no fluctuation.
3. **UKDF and FrDF** report **zero storage utilization** at allocation completion across all their allocations (72 and 144, respectively).
4. Overall, storage is effectively **idle at job allocation time** across the entire grid — no site exceeds 0.03% utilization, suggesting storage pressure is not a bottleneck during the allocation phase.

messages.content:
## File Transfer Volume by Site Pair

The query found **10 distinct source→destination pairs**. Here is a summary ordered by total data moved:

| Source → Destination | Transfers | Total Data (GB) | Avg Duration (s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| USDF → FrDF | 2,003 | 183.4 | 135.2 |
| USDF → UKDF | 847 | 76.7 | 57.2 |
| Base → USDF | 390 | 39.6 | 6.0 |
| Summit → Base | 327 | 26.3 | 2.2 |
| USDF → Base | 138 | 11.4 | 5.1 |
| Base → FrDF | 66 | 6.8 | 10.2 |
| Base → UKDF | 46 | 4.8 | 13.9 |
| Summit → USDF | 32 | 2.5 | 4.9 |
| Summit → FrDF | 9 | 0.74 | 8.6 |
| Summit → UKDF | 6 | 0.49 | 11.5 |

*(GB values are raw bytes ÷ 1,000,000,000 for readability, sourced directly from the `total_bytes` column)*

### Key Observations

- **USDF is the dominant data source**, accounting for the top two pairs by volume. The **USDF → FrDF** lane alone moved **183.4 GB across 2,003 transfers** — by far the largest flow, and also the slowest on average (135 s/transfer).
- **USDF → UKDF** is the second-largest lane (76.7 GB, 847 transfers) with noticeably faster average transfers (~57 s).
- **Summit → Base** is the busiest *non-USDF-source* lane by transfer count (327 transfers) but with very fast average durations (2.2 s), suggesting short-range or high-bandwidth links.
- **Base acts as both a receiver and a forwarder**: it receives from Summit and USDF, then re-distributes to FrDF and UKDF.
- The four smallest pairs (Summit → USDF/FrDF/UKDF and Base → UKDF) collectively account for fewer than 100 transfers and under 8.6 GB total.

What is the total and average job execution cost per site, and how many jobs contributed to that cost?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS job_count, SUM(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cost') AS REAL)) AS total_cost, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cost') AS REAL)) AS avg_cost_per_job FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site ORDER BY total_cost DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Job Execution Cost by Site

| Site | Jobs | Total Cost | Avg Cost/Job |
|------|------|-----------|--------------|
| UKDF | 72 | -72.0 | -1.0 |
| FrDF | 144 | -144.0 | -1.0 |
| Base | 350 | -350.0 | -1.0 |
| USDF | 434 | -434.0 | -1.0 |

### Key Observations

- **Uniform per-job cost:** Every site shows an identical average cost of **-1.0 per job**, regardless of site or scale. This suggests a flat cost model is applied uniformly across the grid.
- **Negative cost values:** All cost figures are negative, which in this simulation model likely represents a credit, charge-back, or consumed budget unit rather than a monetary profit.
- **Largest contributor:** USDF drove the highest absolute cost burden (-434.0) simply because it ran the most jobs (434), followed by Base (350 jobs, -350.0).
- **Smallest contributor:** UKDF had the fewest jobs (72) and the lowest total cost (-72.0).
- **Total across all sites:** The simulation recorded **1,000 finished job executions** across 4 sites, with the aggregate cost scaling directly and linearly with job count at every site — no site incurred premium or discounted rates.

What is the average disk write bandwidth and total bytes written per disk device per site?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk') AS disk, COUNT(*) AS write_ops, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_write_bw') AS REAL)) AS avg_write_bw, SUM(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL)) AS total_bytes_written FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileWrite' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site, disk ORDER BY total_bytes_written DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Disk Write Bandwidth & Volume by Site/Device

Four site–disk pairs recorded write activity across the simulation:

| Site | Disk | Write Ops | Avg Write BW | Total Written |
|------|------|-----------|--------------|---------------|
| USDF | USDF_DISK | 862 | 10 GB/s | ~174.0 GB |
| FrDF | FrDF_DISK | 285 | 10 GB/s | ~93.3 GB |
| UKDF | UKDF_DISK | 152 | 10 GB/s | ~41.1 GB |
| Base | BASE_DISK | 526 | 5 GB/s | ~31.2 GB |

*(GB = values ÷ 1,000,000,000 directly from query results)*

### Key Observations

- **Bandwidth tiers:** Three sites (USDF, FrDF, UKDF) operate at a uniform **10 GB/s** disk write bandwidth, while **Base** runs at half that — **5 GB/s** — making it the bandwidth bottleneck among all sites.
- **Write volume leader:** USDF accounts for the most data written (**173,983,781,524 bytes / ~174.0 GB**) across the highest number of write operations (862), nearly double FrDF's volume.
- **High ops, low volume at Base:** Despite 526 write operations (second highest), Base writes only ~31.2 GB total, suggesting its writes involve many small files — compounded by its lower 5 GB/s bandwidth ceiling.
- **UKDF** has the fewest write operations (152) and the third-largest total volume (~41.1 GB), implying larger average file sizes per write compared to Base.

Per site, how do the average file-transfer queue time, resource-waiting queue time, and total I/O read time compare for finished job executions?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS job_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.file_transfer_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_file_transfer_queue_s, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.resource_waiting_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_resource_waiting_queue_s, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_io_read_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_total_io_read_s, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_total_queue_s FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site ORDER BY avg_total_queue_s DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Per-Site Queue Time & I/O Read Time — Finished Job Executions

### Key Finding: File-Transfer Queue Dominates; Resource-Waiting Queue is Zero Everywhere

Across all 4 sites, **resource-waiting queue time is 0.0 s** universally, meaning no job waited for compute resources. All queuing pressure comes entirely from file-transfer staging.

---

### Site-by-Site Breakdown

| Site | Jobs | Avg File-Transfer Queue (s) | Avg Resource-Waiting Queue (s) | Avg Total I/O Read (s) | Avg Total Queue (s) |
|------|------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------|---------------------|
| **FrDF** | 144 | **105.71** | 0.0 | 0.138 | 105.71 |
| **UKDF** | 72 | **43.03** | 0.0 | 0.121 | 43.03 |
| **Base** | 350 | 2.21 | 0.0 | 0.196 | 2.21 |
| **USDF** | 434 | −0.25 | 0.0 | **3.629** | −0.25 |

---

### Operational Highlights

1. **FrDF is the worst file-transfer bottleneck**: average queue of **105.71 s** per job — roughly **2.5× higher than UKDF** (43.03 s) and **48× higher than Base** (2.21 s).

2. **USDF has negligible file-transfer queuing** (−0.25 s, effectively zero/simulation noise) but stands out for **I/O read time at 3.629 s** — about **18–30× higher** than the other three sites (0.121–0.196 s). This suggests local disk read throughput is the constraint at USDF rather than transfer staging.

3. **Base site** (350 jobs, the largest single-site workload) maintains low queue times (2.21 s) and low I/O read times (0.196 s), indicating it is well-provisioned relative to its load.

4. **Total queue time equals file-transfer queue time at every site**, confirming the zero resource-waiting component is not a data gap but a genuine simulation outcome.

## Effective vs. Stated Throughput for Finished File Transfers

Across all 10 source–destination pairs, **effective throughput (file size ÷ transfer duration) is a tiny fraction of stated link bandwidth** — reflecting real-world overhead from queuing, latency, contention, and small file sizes.

### High-Bandwidth Links (stated: 12,500 MB/s)
| Route | Transfers | Avg Effective (MB/s) | % of Stated BW |
|---|---|---|---|
| Summit → Base | 327 | 37.1 | ~0.30% |
| Base → USDF | 390 | 16.9 | ~0.14% |
| USDF → Base | 138 | 15.8 | ~0.13% |
| Summit → USDF | 32 | 15.8 | ~0.13% |

### Lower-Bandwidth Links (stated: 1,250 MB/s)
| Route | Transfers | Avg Effective (MB/s) | % of Stated BW |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base → FrDF | 66 | 10.0 | ~0.80% |
| Summit → FrDF | 9 | 9.5 | ~0.76% |
| Base → UKDF | 46 | 7.5 | ~0.60% |
| Summit → UKDF | 6 | 7.1 | ~0.57% |
| USDF → UKDF | 847 | 1.6 | ~0.12% |
| USDF → FrDF | 2,003 | 0.7 | ~0.05% |

- **No route exceeds 0.8% of stated bandwidth.** Effective throughput is not a measure of link saturation but of end-to-end transfer efficiency (dominated by overhead for small files).

messages.content:
## Per-Site FileRead vs. FileWrite Duration Comparison

### Key Findings

**Read durations vary far more than write durations across sites:**

| Site | Avg Read Duration (s) | Avg Write Duration (s) | # Reads | # Writes |
|------|-----------------------|------------------------|---------|----------|
| Base | 0.1406 | 0.1171 | 489 | 526 |
| FrDF | 0.0096 | 0.0791 | 2,078 | 285 |
| UKDF | 0.0097 | 0.0769 | 899 | 152 |
| USDF | 0.4263 | 0.0777 | 3,695 | 862 |

### Notable Observations

1. **USDF reads are the slowest** — averaging 0.4263 s, roughly **44× slower** than FrDF/UKDF reads (~0.0096–0.0097 s). Despite this, USDF handles by far the most read operations (3,695).

2. **Write durations are remarkably consistent** — ranging narrowly from 0.0769 s (UKDF) to 0.1171 s (Base), suggesting write performance is more uniform across the grid than read performance.

3. **FrDF and UKDF reads are very fast** (~0.0096–0.0097 s) but their **writes are ~8× slower** than their reads — the reverse pattern of USDF.

4. **Base is the most balanced** — read and write durations are closest to each other (0.1406 s vs. 0.1171 s), and operation counts are also nearly equal (489 reads, 526 writes).

5. **Reads dominate at FrDF, UKDF, and USDF** (7:1, 6:1, and 4:1 read-to-write ratios respectively), while Base is roughly 1:1.

messages.content:
## Link Load Distribution at File Transfer Start

### Key Finding: Link Load is Universally Zero

Across **all 10 source–destination site pairs** observed, the link load at the moment a file transfer starts is **0.0** — without exception. The min, avg, and max are identical (0.0) for every pair.

### Transfer Volume by Route

| Source → Destination | Transfers Started |
|---|---|
| USDF → FrDF | 2,003 |
| USDF → UKDF | 847 |
| Base → USDF | 390 |
| Summit → Base | 327 |
| USDF → Base | 138 |
| Base → FrDF | 66 |
| Base → UKDF | 46 |
| Summit → USDF | 32 |
| Summit → FrDF | 9 |
| Summit → UKDF | 6 |

**Total transfers started: 3,865** across the 10 routes.

### Operational Interpretation

The constant zero link load at transfer start indicates that **no link congestion is being recorded at the moment transfers are initiated** in this simulation. This could mean:
- Links are never saturated when new transfers begin (transfers start during idle periods), or
- The simulation's link load metric is not being populated (all values defaulting to 0).

This warrants verification — if link load tracking is expected to be active, the metric instrumentation may need review.

messages.content:
## Site-Level CPU Utilization at Job Execution Start

The table below summarizes the site CPU utilization recorded at the moment each job execution begins, across 4 sites:

| Site | Jobs Started | Min CPU Util | Avg CPU Util | Max CPU Util |
|------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| **Base** | 350 | 0.005 (0.5%) | 0.1477 (14.8%) | 0.2794 (27.9%) |
| **UKDF** | 72 | 0.0042 (0.4%) | 0.1260 (12.6%) | 0.2115 (21.1%) |
| **USDF** | 434 | 0.0004 (0.04%) | 0.1004 (10.0%) | 0.2288 (22.9%) |
| **FrDF** | 144 | 0.0017 (0.2%) | 0.1004 (10.0%) | 0.1744 (17.4%) |

### Key Observations

- **Base** carries the highest average site CPU load at job start (~14.8%) and also peaks the highest at ~27.9%, despite not being the busiest by job count.
- **USDF** handles the most job starts (434) but maintains a lower average load (~10.0%), suggesting better capacity headroom.
- **UKDF** has the fewest job starts (72) with a mid-range average load (~12.6%).
- **FrDF and USDF** share nearly identical average utilization (~10.0%), but FrDF's maximum (~17.4%) is notably lower than USDF's (~22.9%), indicating more consistent load at FrDF.
- All sites show very low minimum utilization values (near 0%), meaning jobs occasionally start when the site is nearly idle.

messages.content: {"columns": ["hour_bucket", "writes_finished", "avg_grid_storage_util", "max_grid_storage_util"], "rows": [[0, 1825, 0.00010453046689453263, 0.00016256445385809393]], "row_count": 1}

## Grid-Wide Storage Utilization During File Writes

### Key Finding: All Activity Concentrated in a Single Hour

All file write completions occurred within **hour bucket 0** (the first 0–3,600 seconds of simulation time). There is no multi-hour evolution to report — the entire workload of file writes finished within that single interval.

| Hour Bucket | Writes Finished | Avg Grid Storage Util | Max Grid Storage Util |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1,825 | 0.0105% | 0.0163% |

### Observations

- **1,825 file writes** completed in the first hour — this represents the entire dataset; no writes appear in any subsequent hour.
- **Average grid storage utilization** at write completion was just **0.0105%** (≈ 0.000105 as a fraction), indicating the grid's storage was barely touched.
- **Peak utilization** reached only **0.0163%** at most, meaning even at the busiest moment, grid storage capacity was almost entirely free.

### Operational Takeaway

Grid storage is **not a bottleneck** in this simulation. With peak utilization under 0.02% and all writes finishing within the first hour, there is substantial headroom for increased workloads. If storage pressure is a concern in future scenarios, the simulation would need far more concurrent write activity to surface any contention.

## Per-Host Job Execution Summary

The query returned **123 host/site combinations** (results truncated to 25 shown here). Key findings from the visible data:

### Busiest Hosts (by job count)
| Host | Site | Jobs | Avg Duration (s) | Avg Flops |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base_cpu-11 | Base | 32 | 7.95e-8 | 254.5 |
| Base_cpu-19 | Base | 32 | 8.63e-8 | 276.2 |
| Base_cpu-0 | Base | 29 | 9.40e-8 | 428.0 |
| Base_cpu-13 | Base | 29 | 1.01e-7 | 436.3 |
| Base_cpu-14 | Base | 29 | 8.58e-8 | 369.9 |
| Base_cpu-16 | Base | 29 | 9.42e-8 | 399.3 |

### Notable Patterns

- **Base site dominates** the top of the list by job count, with hosts handling 15–32 jobs each and very short durations (~8–16 ns) with low flop counts (~255–8,000 avg flops).
- **USDF, FrDF, and UKDF hosts** handled fewer jobs (8–11 per host) but with substantially higher workloads — e.g., `USDF_cpu-14` averaged **12,715.5 flops/job** at ~6.34e-7 s, and `UKDF_cpu-0` averaged **23,664 flops/job** at ~1.06e-6 s.

- There is a clear **inverse relationship** between job count per host and job complexity (flops/duration) — high-volume hosts run light jobs; low-volume hosts run compute-intensive ones.

messages.content:
## File-Transfer Performance by File-Size Bucket

Only two size buckets appear in the simulation data — **small (<100 MB)** and **medium (100 MB–1 GB)**. No transfers in the large (1–10 GB) or very large (>10 GB) categories were recorded.

| Bucket | Transfer Count | Avg Duration (s) | Max Duration (s) | Avg Throughput (bps) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small (<100 MB) | 2,514 | 73.5 | 149.5 | 7,739,753 |
| Medium (100 MB–1 GB) | 1,350 | 103.7 | 163.1 | 4,231,641 |

### Key Observations

1. **Volume**: Small-file transfers dominate, accounting for 2,514 transfers versus 1,350 for medium files.

2. **Duration**: Medium-file transfers take notably longer on average (103.7 s vs. 73.5 s) and also have a higher maximum duration (163.1 s vs. 149.5 s). However, the gap between the two maximums is relatively narrow (~13.6 s), suggesting the network is similarly saturated in both cases at peak load.

3. **Effective Throughput**: Small files achieve nearly **twice** the average throughput of medium files (≈7.74 Mbps vs. ≈4.23 Mbps). This counter-intuitive result — smaller files transferring more efficiently — likely reflects that small transfers complete quickly before link congestion builds, while medium-file transfers sustain longer periods of shared bandwidth contention.

4. **No large or very large transfers**: The absence of files ≥1 GB suggests the workload modeled consists entirely of relatively modest input/output files.

messages.content:
## CPU Utilization at Job Execution Finish by Core Count

### Site-Level CPU Utilization

| Cores | Jobs | Avg Site CPU Util | Max Site CPU Util |
|-------|------|-------------------|-------------------|
| 1 | 374 | **14.2%** | 24.9% |
| 4 | 374 | **9.6%** | 27.7% |
| 8 | 252 | **11.4%** | 22.8% |

**Key observations:**
- **1-core jobs** carry the highest *average* site CPU utilization (14.2%), suggesting that when many single-core jobs finish, sites are busier on average.
- **4-core jobs** have the lowest average (9.6%) but the highest *peak* site utilization (27.7%), indicating occasional spikes.
- **8-core jobs** sit in the middle for average (11.4%) and have the lowest peak (22.8%), suggesting more predictable, moderate site load.
- There is **no simple monotonic relationship** between core count and site CPU utilization.

### Grid-Level CPU Utilization

All three groups report grid CPU utilization values on the order of **10⁻¹³** (effectively zero), regardless of core count. This means at the moment individual jobs finish, the grid-wide CPU load is negligible in all cases — the simulation's grid is lightly loaded overall, and core count has no meaningful effect on grid-level utilization.

### Summary
Core count primarily influences **site-level** dynamics: single-core jobs sustain higher average site load, while 4-core jobs occasionally drive higher site peaks. Grid-level utilization is uniformly near zero across all core configurations.

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS job_count, ROUND(AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)), 4) AS avg_queue_fraction, ROUND(MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)), 4) AS max_queue_fraction FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site ORDER BY avg_queue_fraction DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Queue Overhead Fraction by Site (Finished Job Executions)

All four sites show queue overhead fractions **far exceeding 1.0**, meaning total queue time dwarfs actual execution duration at every site. This points to severe queuing inefficiency across the grid.

### Site Rankings (Worst to Best)

| Site | Jobs | Avg Queue Fraction | Max Queue Fraction |
|------|------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **FrDF** | 144 | 110,922,083 | 458,544,093 |
| **UKDF** | 72 | 54,764,096 | 155,813,302 |
| **Base** | 350 | 25,276,247 | 51,541,544 |
| **USDF** | 434 | 10,420,866 | 114,613,192 |

### Key Observations

- **FrDF is the worst offender** by a wide margin — its average queue fraction (110.9M) is roughly **2× UKDF**, **4.4× Base**, and **10.6× USDF**. Its single worst job reached a fraction of 458.5M.
- **USDF is the most efficient** site with the lowest average (10.4M) despite having the largest job count (434 jobs), suggesting better resource scheduling relative to workload.
- **UKDF** has the smallest job count (72) yet ranks second-worst, indicating a structural queuing problem not simply explained by volume.
- **Base**, despite handling the second-largest volume (350 jobs), maintains a relatively moderate average (25.3M), though its maximum (51.5M) is capped well below the other sites' peaks.

### Operational Takeaway
FrDF and UKDF should be prioritized for scheduling and resource provisioning review, as jobs spend orders of magnitude more time waiting than executing at those sites.

## Disk Write Bandwidth Analysis — Hourly Buckets

### Summary

All 1,825 finished FileWrite operations occurred within a **single hourly bucket (hour 0)**, meaning the entire disk write workload was concentrated in the first hour of the simulation. There is no multi-hour evolution to observe — this represents a single period of sustained write pressure.

### Hour 0 Metrics

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Write operations | 1,825 |
| Average write bandwidth | ~8.56 GB/s |
| Peak (max) write bandwidth | 10.0 GB/s |
| Total data written | ~339.57 GB |

### Key Observations

1. **Single peak period:** All disk write activity is compressed into hour 0, making it both the only period and the peak period of write pressure.

2. **High sustained throughput:** The average bandwidth of ~8.56 GB/s is 85.6% of the observed maximum of 10.0 GB/s, indicating writes were consistently near the ceiling rather than sporadic bursts — a sign of sustained, heavy I/O load throughout this window.

3. **Near-saturated ceiling:** The maximum of exactly 10.0 GB/s suggests a configured disk bandwidth cap is being reached, meaning at least some operations hit the hardware/simulation limit.

4. **Operational implication:** With ~339.57 GB written across 1,825 operations and no activity in subsequent hours, this workload exhibits a sharp, front-loaded write pattern — storage systems must be provisioned to handle this burst at hour 0 without relief from temporal spreading.

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS total_jobs, ROUND(AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cores') AS REAL)), 2) AS avg_cores, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cores') AS INTEGER)) AS max_cores, SUM(CASE WHEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cores') AS INTEGER) > 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS multi_core_jobs, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cores') AS INTEGER) > 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS multi_core_pct FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site ORDER BY avg_cores DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Per-Site Parallelism Patterns — Finished Job Executions

Four sites are represented across 4 rows of results, covering all finished job executions.

### Summary Table

| Site | Total Jobs | Avg Cores | Max Cores | Multi-Core Jobs | Multi-Core % |
|------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------------|--------------|
| **FrDF** | 144 | 5.81 | 8 | 135 | 93.75% |
| **UKDF** | 72 | 5.64 | 8 | 66 | 91.67% |
| **USDF** | 434 | 5.06 | 8 | 402 | 92.63% |
| **Base** | 350 | 1.28 | 8 | 23 | 6.57% |

### Key Observations

1. **FrDF, UKDF, and USDF are heavily parallel sites.** All three average well above 5 cores per job and have multi-core rates above 91%. FrDF leads with an average of 5.81 cores and 93.75% of its 144 jobs running multi-core.

2. **USDF carries the highest job volume** (434 jobs) while still maintaining strong parallelism (5.06 avg cores, 92.63% multi-core).

3. **Base is predominantly single-core.** Despite running 350 jobs, only 23 (6.57%) used more than one core, and its average core count is just 1.28. It appears to be used for lightweight or serial workloads.

4. **All sites share the same maximum of 8 cores**, suggesting a common upper limit across the grid — but Base almost never reaches it in practice.

### Operational Takeaway
The three data-facility sites (FrDF, UKDF, USDF) are operating in a highly parallel mode; any scheduling or resource contention issues there will be amplified by multi-core demand. Base is effectively a single-core workhorse and would not benefit significantly from multi-core tuning.

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk') AS disk, MIN(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS min_read_duration_sec, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS avg_read_duration_sec, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS max_read_duration_sec, COUNT(DISTINCT json_extract(METADATA, '$.file')) AS distinct_files_read, COUNT(*) AS total_read_operations FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileRead' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site, disk ORDER BY avg_read_duration_sec DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## FileRead Performance by Disk Device — I/O Bottleneck Assessment

Four site/disk pairs were active, ordered here from slowest to fastest average read duration:

| Site | Disk | Min (s) | Avg (s) | Max (s) | Distinct Files | Total Reads |
|------|------|---------|---------|---------|----------------|-------------|
| USDF | USDF_DISK | 0.00586 | **0.4263** | **1.2178** | 3,695 | 3,695 |
| Base | BASE_DISK | 0.00687 | 0.1406 | 0.5582 | 489 | 489 |
| UKDF | UKDF_DISK | 0.00310 | 0.00973 | 0.06391 | 899 | 899 |
| FrDF | FrDF_DISK | 0.00243 | 0.00956 | 0.06536 | 2,078 | 2,078 |

### Key Findings

1. **USDF_DISK is the primary bottleneck.** Its average read duration of **0.4263 s** is ~44× slower than UKDF_DISK and FrDF_DISK. Its maximum of **1.2178 s** is the highest across all disks, and it handled the largest workload — **3,695 reads** covering 3,695 distinct files. The combination of high volume and slow throughput makes this the most operationally critical disk.

2. **BASE_DISK is a secondary concern.** At an average of **0.1406 s** and a peak of **0.5582 s**, it is notably slower than UKDF and FrDF, though it served a much smaller volume (489 reads).

3. **UKDF_DISK and FrDF_DISK are healthy.** Both average under **0.010 s** per read and their maximums stay below **0.066 s**, indicating no I/O saturation despite FrDF handling 2,078 reads.

### Operational Recommendation
Prioritize investigation of **USDF_DISK** — its average latency is ~3× worse than BASE_DISK and ~44× worse than the two well-performing disks, while carrying the heaviest read load. Possible causes include disk saturation, slow storage hardware, or I/O contention from concurrent reads.

All four sites share an identical average stated CPU speed of **3,200,000,000 flops/s (3.2 GFlops/s)**, making cross-site efficiency comparisons clean.

| **USDF** | 434 | 16.19 | 25.60 | 3.20 | 22,676 |
| **Base** | 350 | 4.09 | 25.60 | 3.20 | 1,732 |

- **FrDF, UKDF, USDF** all achieve average effective rates (18.6, 18.0, and 16.2 GFlops/s respectively) **far exceeding** the 3.2 GFlops/s single-core stated speed, indicating these jobs are running across multiple cores simultaneously. The maximum of **25.6 GFlops/s** is consistent across all three sites and likely represents the per-job core ceiling.

- **Base site** is the outlier: its average effective rate of **4.09 GFlops/s** is only modestly above the stated single-core speed of 3.2 GFlops/s, suggesting Base jobs run with far fewer cores or much lighter workloads (average flops/job of just **1,732** vs. 22,676–36,890 at other sites).

- **FrDF leads** in average effective rate despite having fewer jobs (144) than USDF (434), and processes the heaviest average workload per job (**36,890 flops**).

- **USDF** handles the largest job volume (434 jobs) at a respectable 16.19 GFlops/s average, but its lower average flops/job (22,676) pulls the site-level rate below FrDF and UKDF.

messages.content:
## Queuing Overhead Analysis: I/O Staging vs. Compute Contention

### Headline Finding: File-Transfer Queuing Dominates Completely — Everywhere

Across all four sites, **100% of total queue time is attributable to file-transfer queuing**. The average and maximum `file_transfer_queue_fraction` is **1.0** at every site, and **resource-waiting queue time is exactly 0.0 seconds** at all sites. Compute-resource contention contributes nothing to queuing overhead in this simulation.

---

### Per-Site Breakdown

| Site | Jobs | Avg FT Queue Time | Resource Wait Time | FT Fraction |
|------|------|-------------------|--------------------|-------------|
| **FrDF** | 144 | **105.71 sec** | 0.0 sec | 1.0 |
| **UKDF** | 72 | 43.03 sec | 0.0 sec | 1.0 |
| **Base** | 350 | 2.21 sec | 0.0 sec | 1.0 |
| **USDF** | 434 | −0.25 sec ⚠️ | 0.0 sec | 1.0 |

---

### Key Operational Takeaways

1. **I/O staging is the sole driver of queueing.** No site shows any resource-waiting overhead — the grid is not compute-constrained in this scenario.
2. **FrDF carries the heaviest I/O staging burden** at an average of 105.71 seconds per job, roughly 2.5× higher than UKDF (43.03 sec) and ~48× higher than Base (2.21 sec).
3. **USDF shows an anomalous negative average FT queue time (−0.25 sec)** across its 434 jobs. While the fraction still resolves to 1.0 (both numerator and denominator are near-zero or negative), this value warrants investigation as a potential data or instrumentation artifact rather than a real operational signal.
4. **Optimization priority:** Since resource waiting is zero everywhere, any effort to reduce total queue time should focus entirely on accelerating file staging — particularly at FrDF and UKDF.

messages.content:
## Grid Data Flow: Sources vs. Sinks

Across all 5 sites, the grid splits cleanly into **3 net exporters** and **2 pure importers** (the French and UK data facilities receive data only).

### Net Exporters

| Site | Sent (GB) | Received (GB) | Net Balance (GB) | Outgoing Transfers | Incoming Transfers |
|------|-----------|--------------|-----------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| **USDF** | 271.5 | 42.1 | **+229.4** | 2,988 | 422 |
| **Summit** | 30.0 | 0 | **+30.0** | 374 | 0 |
| **Base** | 51.2 | 37.7 | **+13.5** | 502 | 465 |

- **USDF** is by far the dominant data source — it accounts for nearly all outgoing volume and runs a 7:1 send-to-receive ratio by bytes.
- **Summit** is a pure one-way source with zero incoming transfers.
- **Base** is roughly balanced in transfer *count* (502 out vs. 465 in) but still a modest net exporter by volume.

### Net Importers (Pure Sinks)

| Site | Sent (GB) | Received (GB) | Net Balance (GB) | Outgoing Transfers | Incoming Transfers |
|------|-----------|--------------|-----------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| **FrDF** | 0 | 190.9 | **−190.9** | 0 | 2,078 |
| **UKDF** | 0 | 82.0 | **−82.0** | 0 | 899 |

- Both **FrDF** and **UKDF** send nothing — they are pure data sinks receiving 190.9 GB and 82.0 GB respectively.
- FrDF is the single largest volume receiver and drives the highest incoming transfer count (2,078).

### Key Takeaway
The grid exhibits a **hub-and-spoke export pattern**: USDF acts as the primary data hub dispatching 271.5 GB across 2,988 transfers, with FrDF and UKDF acting as terminal consumers absorbing a combined 272.9 GB without contributing any outbound data.

messages.content:
## Finished FileRead Performance by Site

Four sites are active. Every read operation involves a unique file (distinct files = read operations in all cases), indicating no file was read twice at the same site.

| Site | Read Ops | Distinct Files | Total Data Read | Min BW | Avg BW | Max BW |
|------|----------|----------------|-----------------|--------|--------|--------|
| **USDF** | 3,695 | 3,695 | ~329.3 GB | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s |
| **FrDF** | 2,078 | 2,078 | ~190.9 GB | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s |
| **UKDF** | 899 | 899 | ~82.0 GB | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s |
| **Base** | 489 | 489 | ~40.1 GB | 5 GB/s | 5 GB/s | 5 GB/s |

*(GB = bytes ÷ 1,000,000,000)*

### Key Operational Findings

1. **No intra-site variation anywhere.** At every site, min = avg = max read bandwidth, meaning disk performance is perfectly uniform — no jitter, no outliers, no degraded reads within any site.

2. **Base is the slow site.** Its disk read bandwidth is **5 GB/s**, exactly half the 10 GB/s delivered by USDF, FrDF, and UKDF. This is a structural difference (likely a slower disk tier configured at Base), not a transient issue, since bandwidth never deviates from 5 GB/s across all 489 operations.

3. **USDF carries the heaviest read load** at 3,695 operations and ~329.3 GB, followed by FrDF (~190.9 GB), UKDF (~82.0 GB), and Base (~40.1 GB).

4. **No site shows inconsistent performance** — the concern is solely Base's consistently lower throughput, which will systematically slow any jobs that are disk-read-bound at that site.

## Job Execution Start Rate vs. Grid CPU Utilization

### Coverage
The query returns **1 simulation hour** of data (hour 0 only), meaning all recorded job execution starts fall within the first hour of the simulation.

### Key Findings

| Simulation Hour | Jobs Started | Min Grid CPU Util | Avg Grid CPU Util | Max Grid CPU Util |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | **1,000** | ~9.74 × 10⁻¹⁶ | ~2.45 × 10⁻¹³ | ~4.73 × 10⁻¹³ |

### Interpretation

- **All 1,000 job executions begin in hour 0**, indicating an immediate, concentrated submission burst at simulation start rather than a distributed ramp-up over time.
- **Grid CPU utilization at job-start moments is effectively zero** across all three measures (min, avg, max are all on the order of 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹⁶). This is consistent with a cold-start scenario: jobs are being dispatched before any meaningful CPU work has accumulated on the grid.

### Operational Takeaway
The simulation essentially front-loads all job submissions into hour 0 against an idle grid. If multiple simulation hours were present, you could track whether later submission waves correlate with elevated CPU utilization; with only hour 0 available, the data shows a cold-start burst with no measurable prior grid load.

messages.content:
## Per-Site I/O-to-Duration Ratio Analysis

All four sites show **total_io_read_time far exceeding wall-clock job duration** (all ratios >> 1), indicating that `total_io_read_time` is an accumulated metric summed across all parallel I/O operations within a job — not a simple fraction. With that framing, higher ratios mean more cumulative I/O activity relative to elapsed time.

### Site Rankings (by Average Ratio, descending)

| Site | Jobs | Avg Ratio | Min Ratio | Max Ratio |
|------|------|-----------|-----------|-----------|

| **UKDF** | 72 | 77,160 | 24,855 | 166,043 |
| **FrDF** | 144 | 76,417 | 11,521 | 187,441 |

### Key Observations

messages.content:
## Finished File Transfers: Latency & Duration by Source Site

Three source sites were observed across **3,864 total finished file transfers**.

| Source Site | Transfers | Avg Latency (s) | Min Latency (s) | Max Latency (s) | Avg Transfer Duration (s) |
|-------------|-----------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|---------------------------|
| **USDF** | 2,988 | 0.1255 | 0.095 | 0.130 | 107.11 |
| **Base** | 502 | 0.1145 | 0.095 | 0.215 | 7.25 |
| **Summit** | 374 | 0.0164 | 0.001 | 0.216 | 2.71 |

### Key Findings

- **USDF is the highest-latency source site** by average, at **0.1255 s**, and its latency range is notably tight (0.095–0.130 s), meaning it *consistently* experiences elevated latency — there is little variation. This consistency makes USDF the most reliably high-latency origin.
- **Base** is second at **0.1145 s** average, but shows a wider spread (up to 0.215 s), suggesting occasional spikes rather than uniform congestion.
- **Summit** has by far the lowest average latency at **0.0164 s**, though its maximum (0.216 s) hints at rare outlier events.
- The transfer duration pattern mirrors latency rank: USDF's average duration (**107.11 s**) is roughly **15× longer** than Base's (7.25 s) and **40× longer** than Summit's (2.71 s), indicating that USDF's outgoing data movements are both the slowest and the most numerous.

### Operational Takeaway
USDF warrants priority attention for network optimization — it accounts for 77% of all outgoing transfers, has the highest and most stable latency, and its average transfer time of over 107 seconds is a significant bottleneck compared to the other sites.

messages.content:
## Finished FileWrite Performance by Site

**Four sites** recorded finished FileWrite operations. Across all of them, disk write bandwidth shows **zero intra-site variability** (min = max = avg at every site), so the key differentiator is the absolute bandwidth tier.

### Site-by-Site Summary

| Site | Writes | Distinct Files | Avg BW | Min BW | Max BW | Total Written |
|------|--------|----------------|--------|--------|--------|---------------|
| Base | 526 | 526 | 5 GB/s | 5 GB/s | 5 GB/s | ~31.2 GB |
| FrDF | 285 | 285 | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | ~93.3 GB |
| UKDF | 152 | 152 | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | ~41.1 GB |
| USDF | 862 | 862 | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | 10 GB/s | ~174.0 GB |

*(Bandwidth values read directly from results: 5,000,000,000 B/s and 10,000,000,000 B/s; totals converted from raw bytes)*

### Key Findings

- **Weakest site — Base**: Its disk write bandwidth (5 GB/s) is exactly **half** that of every other site. Despite handling 526 writes — the second-highest volume — it is the clear performance bottleneck for write operations.
- **No variability anywhere**: Every site's min and max bandwidth are identical to its average, meaning write performance is perfectly flat within each site. There are no outliers or degraded individual writes to investigate.
- **Highest workload — USDF**: With 862 writes and ~174 GB of data written, USDF carries the largest write burden, yet sustains the full 10 GB/s tier.
- **Each file written exactly once**: At every site, `distinct_files` = `write_count`, confirming no file was written more than once at the same site.

### Operational Recommendation
Base is the sole site warranting attention — not for variability, but for its consistently lower write tier. If Base is on a critical path for output staging, upgrading its storage bandwidth to match the 10 GB/s standard of the other three sites would directly reduce write-phase latency there.

For each unique source→destination site pair in finished file transfers, how many transfers occurred, what was the total bytes moved, what were the average and maximum effective throughput (size divided by duration), and what was the average link load — mapping inter-site data corridor efficiency and congestion?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.source_site') AS source_site, json_extract(METADATA, '$.destination_site') AS destination_site, COUNT(*) AS transfer_count, SUM(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL)) AS total_bytes_transferred, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)) AS avg_effective_throughput, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)) AS max_effective_throughput, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.link_load') AS REAL)) AS avg_link_load FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileTransfer' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY source_site, destination_site ORDER BY total_bytes_transferred DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Inter-Site File Transfer Corridor Analysis

10 unique source→destination pairs are active. All throughput and link-load figures are in MB/s (÷ 1,000,000 from raw bytes/s); totals are in GB.

---

### Volume & Transfer Counts (ranked by total bytes)

| Corridor | Transfers | Total (GB) |
|---|---|---|
| USDF → FrDF | 2,003 | 183.4 |
| USDF → UKDF | 847 | 76.7 |
| Base → USDF | 390 | 39.6 |
| Summit → Base | 327 | 26.3 |
| USDF → Base | 138 | 11.4 |
| Base → FrDF | 66 | 6.8 |
| Base → UKDF | 46 | 4.8 |
| Summit → USDF | 32 | 2.5 |
| Summit → FrDF | 9 | 0.74 |
| Summit → UKDF | 6 | 0.49 |

---

### Throughput & Congestion Efficiency

| Corridor | Avg Throughput (MB/s) | Max Throughput (MB/s) | Avg Link Load (MB/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| USDF → FrDF | **0.67** | 1.16 | 1,227 |
| USDF → UKDF | 1.55 | 2.89 | 1,200 |
| Base → USDF | 16.87 | 18.76 | 5,530 |
| Summit → Base | **37.06** | **48.13** | 12,410 |
| USDF → Base | 15.83 | 18.23 | 7,828 |
| Base → FrDF | 10.04 | 10.98 | 461 |
| Base → UKDF | 7.51 | 8.11 | 241 |
| Summit → USDF | 15.81 | 16.45 | 378 |
| Summit → FrDF | 9.54 | 9.75 | 68 |
| Summit → UKDF | 7.11 | 7.38 | 36 |

---

### Key Operational Findings

1. **Dominant corridor — severely throttled:** USDF → FrDF carries by far the most data (183.4 GB, 2,003 transfers) yet delivers the worst effective throughput (avg **0.67 MB/s**, max 1.16 MB/s), against a link load of **1,227 MB/s**. The extreme disparity between link load and effective throughput signals heavy congestion or significant queuing on this path.

2. **USDF → UKDF** is similarly degraded (avg 1.55 MB/s, link load 1,200 MB/s), despite being the second-busiest corridor by volume.

3. **Best-performing corridor:** Summit → Base achieves the highest avg throughput (**37.06 MB/s**) and peak throughput (**48.13 MB/s**), though it also carries the highest average link load (12,410 MB/s), suggesting a high-capacity but heavily loaded internal link.

4. **Internal vs. external split:** All corridors involving FrDF or UKDF as destinations show markedly lower effective throughput (0.67–10.04 MB/s) and much lower link loads (36–1,227 MB/s) compared to intra-cluster paths (Base↔USDF, Summit↔Base), consistent with wide-area network bottlenecks on inter-continental links.

5. **Low-volume tail:** The Summit → FrDF (9 transfers) and Summit → UKDF (6 transfers) corridors are rarely used and show very low link loads (68 and 36 MB/s respectively), suggesting spare capacity or infrequent activation.

Per site, how do the average file_transfer_queue_time, resource_waiting_queue_time, and total_queue_time compare between retried and non-retried finished job executions — revealing whether retried jobs suffer disproportionate queuing delays and which queue component dominates?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, CASE WHEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.retries') AS INTEGER) = 0 THEN 'no_retry' ELSE 'retried' END AS retry_group, COUNT(*) AS job_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.file_transfer_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_file_transfer_queue_time, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.resource_waiting_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_resource_waiting_queue_time, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_total_queue_time, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS max_total_queue_time FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site, retry_group ORDER BY site, retry_group LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Key Finding: No Retried Jobs Exist

The most important result is that **zero retried jobs appear in any site** — all four sites have only a `no_retry` group. A retried vs. non-retried comparison is therefore impossible with this data.

---

## Queue Time Breakdown by Site (No-Retry Jobs Only)

| Site | Jobs | Avg File Transfer Queue | Avg Resource Waiting | Avg Total Queue | Max Total Queue |
|------|------|------------------------|---------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Base | 350 | 2.21 s | 0.0 s | 2.21 s | 7.95 s |
| FrDF | 144 | 105.71 s | 0.0 s | 105.71 s | 162.76 s |
| UKDF | 72 | 43.03 s | 0.0 s | 43.03 s | 71.67 s |
| USDF | 434 | −0.25 s | 0.0 s | −0.25 s | 9.95 s |

---

## Operational Observations

1. **File transfer queue time is the sole queue component.** Resource waiting queue time is **0.0 s** at every site, so file transfer queuing fully explains total queue time everywhere.

2. **FrDF is the heaviest queue burden** — average total queue time of **105.71 s**, peaking at **162.76 s**. This is ~2.5× worse than UKDF (43.03 s avg) and ~48× worse than Base (2.21 s avg).

3. **USDF shows a marginally negative average (−0.25 s)**, which is a simulation artifact (near-zero values with floating-point noise); operationally treat it as ~0 s.

4. **No retry pressure exists** — since retries = 0 across all 1,000 total jobs, there is no evidence that queuing delays are triggering job failures or retries in this simulation run.

| Metric | Value |

messages.content:
## 10 Most Queue-Delayed Finished Job Executions

### Summary Findings

**All 10 jobs ran exclusively at site FrDF** — this is a clear site-level concentration of delay.

### Delay Breakdown

| JOB_ID | Total Queue (s) | File-Transfer Queue (s) | Resource-Waiting (s) | Duration (s) | Queue % of Duration | Retries |
|--------|----------------|------------------------|----------------------|--------------|---------------------|---------|
| 123 | 162.758 | 162.758 | 0.0 | 2.76e-06 | 5,897,037,136.92% | 0 |
| 67 | 162.657 | 162.657 | 0.0 | 6.16e-06 | 2,639,196,987.68% | 0 |
| 314 | 162.601 | 162.601 | 0.0 | 2.70e-06 | 6,026,443,386.70% | 0 |
| 179 | 161.785 | 161.785 | 0.0 | 4.07e-06 | 3,979,963,003.77% | 0 |
| 298 | 161.565 | 161.565 | 0.0 | 6.23e-07 | 25,915,204,092.55% | 0 |
| 423 | 161.302 | 161.302 | 0.0 | 3.33e-06 | 4,843,907,423.20% | 0 |
| 560 | 161.297 | 161.297 | 0.0 | 3.19e-06 | 5,052,852,873.86% | 0 |
| 293 | 161.129 | 161.129 | 0.0 | 5.22e-06 | 3,086,767,515.16% | 0 |
| 182 | 161.002 | 161.002 | 0.0 | 3.35e-06 | 4,806,468,885.69% | 0 |
| 959 | 160.913 | 160.913 | 0.0 | 2.98e-06 | 5,395,808,549.45% | 0 |

### Key Operational Takeaways

1. **Dominant delay cause: file-transfer queue time — exclusively.** For all 10 jobs, `resource_waiting_queue_time = 0.0`, meaning 100% of queue time was driven by file-transfer contention, not CPU/slot availability.

2. **Queue time dwarfs actual compute duration.** Actual execution durations are in the **microsecond range** (e.g., job 298 at 6.23e-07 s), while queue times are ~161–163 seconds. The queue-to-duration percentages reach into the **billions of percent**, most extreme for job 298 at 25,915,204,092.55%.

3. **Zero retries across all 10 jobs** — these delays were not caused by failures or re-executions; the jobs completed on the first attempt after an extremely long wait.

## Cost-Per-Flop Analysis by Site (Finished Job Executions)

### Key Observation on Cost Values
All cost values are negative (each job carries a cost of exactly –1 unit, regardless of site), so cost-per-flop figures are also negative. A value **closer to zero** means fewer cost units consumed per flop delivered — i.e., more computational bang per unit cost.

---

### Site Summary Table

| Site | Jobs | Total Cost | Total Flops | Avg Cost/Flop | Min Cost/Flop | Max Cost/Flop |
|------|------|-----------|-------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| **Base** | 350 | –350.0 | 606,252 | –0.003626 | –0.007246 | –0.0000089 |
| **USDF** | 434 | –434.0 | 9,841,494 | –0.000417 | –0.006410 | –0.0000053 |
| **UKDF** | 72 | –72.0 | 2,241,831 | –0.000376 | –0.004386 | –0.0000078 |
| **FrDF** | 144 | –144.0 | 5,312,118 | –0.000324 | –0.004444 | –0.0000063 |

---

### Efficiency Verdict

- 🏆 **Most cost-efficient: FrDF** — avg cost/flop of **–0.000324**, the least negative value, meaning it delivers the most flops per unit of cost. It processed 5,312,118 flops across 144 jobs at a total cost of –144.0.

- **USDF** dominates in raw throughput (9,841,494 total flops across 434 jobs) and sits near the efficient end (–0.000417 avg cost/flop), making it the highest-volume and near-efficient option.
