messages.content:
## Compute Speed and Duration vs. Core Count, by Site

### Compute Speed: Completely Flat
Every site and every core configuration records exactly **3,200,000,000.0 operations/s (3.2 GHz)**. Core count has zero effect on the speed metric — the hardware allocation is homogeneous across the entire grid.

---

### Duration: Higher Core Count → Longer Completions (Consistently)

All durations are in seconds:

| Site | Cores | Jobs | Avg Duration (s) | Min Duration (s) | Max Duration (s) |
|------|-------|------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Base | 1 | 511 | 8.37 × 10⁻⁸ | 3.94 × 10⁻⁸ | 1.52 × 10⁻⁷ |
| Base | 4 | 31 | 4.37 × 10⁻⁷ | 2.07 × 10⁻⁷ | 8.98 × 10⁻⁷ |
| Base | 8 | 2 | 3.99 × 10⁻⁶ | 3.18 × 10⁻⁶ | 4.81 × 10⁻⁶ |
| FrDF | 1 | 19 | 8.10 × 10⁻⁸ | 5.91 × 10⁻⁸ | 1.04 × 10⁻⁷ |
| FrDF | 4 | 78 | 4.59 × 10⁻⁷ | 1.87 × 10⁻⁷ | 7.76 × 10⁻⁷ |
| FrDF | 8 | 109 | 2.54 × 10⁻⁶ | 4.83 × 10⁻⁷ | 7.87 × 10⁻⁶ |
| UKDF | 1 | 14 | 8.32 × 10⁻⁸ | 5.91 × 10⁻⁸ | 1.36 × 10⁻⁷ |
| UKDF | 4 | 65 | 4.67 × 10⁻⁷ | 2.62 × 10⁻⁷ | 9.00 × 10⁻⁷ |
| UKDF | 8 | 47 | 2.70 × 10⁻⁶ | 3.22 × 10⁻⁷ | 6.01 × 10⁻⁶ |
| USDF | 1 | 68 | 8.30 × 10⁻⁸ | 4.78 × 10⁻⁸ | 1.28 × 10⁻⁷ |
| USDF | 4 | 366 | 4.38 × 10⁻⁷ | 1.89 × 10⁻⁷ | 9.39 × 10⁻⁷ |
| USDF | 8 | 190 | 2.51 × 10⁻⁶ | 3.52 × 10⁻⁷ | 8.26 × 10⁻⁶ |

---

### Key Operational Takeaways

1. **More cores do NOT mean faster completions** — the opposite is true at every site. 8-core jobs consistently post the highest average durations, while 1-core jobs are the fastest.

2. **The pattern is universal across all four sites** (Base, FrDF, UKDF, USDF), suggesting this is not a site-specific anomaly but a workload characteristic: multi-core slots are assigned to heavier, more compute-intensive jobs.

3. **Wide variance in 8-core jobs**: At USDF, 8-core durations range from 3.52 × 10⁻⁷ s to 8.26 × 10⁻⁶ s — more than a 20× spread — indicating significant heterogeneity in the workload assigned to those slots.

4. **Job distribution is skewed**: USDF runs the most 4-core jobs (366), FrDF and USDF dominate 8-core jobs (109 and 190 respectively), while Base is predominantly single-core (511 of its 544 jobs).

messages.content:
## Network Latency by Source–Destination Corridor

Across all 10 completed file-transfer corridors, **latency is fixed per corridor** — the average and maximum latency are identical in every row, meaning there is no within-corridor latency variation. All latency variation is structural (topology-driven), not load-driven.

### High-Latency Corridors (top 6)

| Corridor | Transfers | Avg/Max Latency | Avg File Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Summit → UKDF | 14 | **0.216** | 82.5 MB |
| Base → UKDF | 86 | **0.215** | 98.1 MB |
| Summit → FrDF | 19 | 0.161 | 82.1 MB |
| Base → FrDF | 89 | 0.160 | 101.5 MB |
| USDF → FrDF | 2,845 | 0.130 | 91.6 MB |
| USDF → UKDF | 1,173 | 0.120 | 91.8 MB |

The transatlantic/intercontinental routes — anything terminating at **UKDF or FrDF** — dominate the high-latency end. **UKDF** is the highest-latency destination regardless of source.

### Low-Latency Corridors
**Summit → Base** stands apart with a latency of just **0.001**, over 200× lower than the top corridors, indicating a local or near-local network path. The mid-tier group (USDF↔Base, Summit→USDF, Base→USDF) clusters around **0.095–0.096**.

### Latency vs. File Size: No Meaningful Correlation
File sizes are remarkably uniform across all corridors, ranging from **~79.1 MB** (Summit→Base) to **~101.6 MB** (Base→USDF) — a spread of only ~22 MB. Meanwhile, latency swings from 0.001 to 0.216. The highest-latency corridors (Summit/Base → UKDF) do **not** carry the largest files, and the largest files (Base→USDF at 101.6 MB, Base→FrDF at 101.5 MB) sit at very different latency levels (0.095 vs. 0.160). **Latency is determined by the geographic corridor, not by the size of the data being moved.**

## File Transfer Bandwidth Utilization: All Corridors Are Severely Under-Provisioned

Across all **10 source–destination site pairs**, actual transfer throughput is a tiny fraction of nominal bandwidth — utilization ratios range from **0.05% to only 0.80%**. No corridor comes close to its provisioned capacity.

---

| Nominal BW | Corridors |
|---|---|

| 4 | USDF → Base | 90 | 16.4 | 12,500 | 0.13% |
| 5 | USDF → UKDF | 1,173 | 1.9 | 1,250 | 0.15% |

### Key Operational Takeaways

1. **USDF→FrDF is the critical outlier**: With 2,845 completed transfers (the highest volume of any corridor) achieving only **0.57 MB/s** against a 1,250 MB/s nominal link, its 0.05% utilization is **3× worse** than the next-worst corridor. This strongly suggests persistent congestion, queuing, or small file overhead on that specific link.

## File Transfer Link Load by Source–Destination Corridor

The query covers **10 distinct corridors** across all started file transfers. Link-load values below are converted to **GB/s** (raw values are in bytes/s) for readability.

---

### Top Congested Corridors (by Average Link Load at Transfer Start)

| Corridor | Transfers Initiated | Avg Link Load | Max Link Load |
|---|---|---|---|
| **USDF → Base** | 90 | **10.69 GB/s** | 12.50 GB/s |
| **Summit → Base** | 511 | **5.85 GB/s** | 12.50 GB/s |
| USDF → UKDF | 1,173 | 0.52 GB/s | 1.25 GB/s |
| USDF → FrDF | 2,845 | 0.28 GB/s | 1.25 GB/s |
| Base → UKDF | 86 | 0.11 GB/s | 0.42 GB/s |
| Base → FrDF | 89 | 0.06 GB/s | 0.77 GB/s |
| Summit → FrDF | 19 | 0.030 GB/s | 0.21 GB/s |
| Summit → UKDF | 14 | 0.020 GB/s | 0.071 GB/s |
| Base → USDF | 529 | 0.0 GB/s | 0.0 GB/s |
| Summit → USDF | 68 | 0.0 GB/s | 0.0 GB/s |

---

### Key Operational Findings

1. **Most congested corridor: USDF → Base.** Despite only 90 transfers initiated, the average link load at start was **10.69 GB/s** and peaked at **12.50 GB/s** — essentially saturating what appears to be a 100 Gbps (12.5 GB/s) link. This is by far the highest average congestion of any corridor.

2. **Summit → Base** is the second most congested (avg **5.85 GB/s**, max **12.50 GB/s**) and carries a much higher volume — **511 transfers** — meaning sustained high load with periodic full saturation.

3. **Both → Base corridors** share the same 12.50 GB/s peak, suggesting a bottleneck at the Base site's inbound link capacity.

4. **USDF → UKDF and USDF → FrDF** are high-volume corridors (1,173 and 2,845 transfers respectively) but operate well within capacity (avg ≤ 0.52 GB/s), indicating headroom remains.

5. **Base → USDF** (529 transfers) and **Summit → USDF** (68 transfers) show **zero link load at initiation**, suggesting these corridors are either uncontested or load is not recorded for outbound Base/Summit traffic toward USDF.

**Priority action:** Monitor and potentially throttle the USDF → Base and Summit → Base corridors, as both regularly hit the apparent link ceiling of 12.5 GB/s.

For each job, how many FileRead operations completed and what was the total bytes read — surfacing the most I/O-intensive jobs in the simulation?

arguments.sql: SELECT JOB_ID, COUNT(*) AS read_count, SUM(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL)) AS total_bytes_read, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS avg_read_duration_sec FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileRead' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY JOB_ID ORDER BY total_bytes_read DESC LIMIT 20

messages.content:
## FileRead I/O Summary — Top 20 Most Intensive Jobs

### Volume Leaders
The top job by total data read is **Job 699**, which completed **50 FileRead operations** totalling **5.28 GB**, with a fast average read duration of **~0.011 seconds**. The next two runners-up are:
- **Job 656**: 50 reads, **5.20 GB**, ~0.010 s avg
- **Job 1427**: 49 reads, **5.13 GB**, ~0.011 s avg

All 20 jobs in this list read between **4.68 GB and 5.28 GB**, a relatively tight range suggesting similar workload profiles.

### Read Count
Most jobs completed either **47, 48, 49, or 50** FileRead operations. No job in this list exceeded 50 reads, and the minimum was 47 (Jobs 257, 162, 1206, 862, 467).

### Notable I/O Latency Outliers
While most jobs show average read durations around **0.010 seconds**, a subset stands out with significantly slower reads:
| Job | Avg Read Duration |
|-----|------------------|
| 553 | 0.904 s |
| 1073 | 0.677 s |
| 566 | 0.666 s |
| 853 | 0.597 s |
| 80 | 0.528 s |

These jobs read comparable total volumes (4.72–5.02 GB) but their per-read latency is **50–90× higher** than the fast-read jobs — a signal of potential disk contention or slower storage at those sites.

### Takeaway
I/O volume is fairly uniform across the top 20 jobs; the real differentiator is **read latency**, with roughly half the list showing sub-15 ms reads and the other half showing 0.44–0.90 s reads, suggesting two distinct storage performance tiers in the simulation.

At the moment job executions start, what are the minimum, average, and maximum site-level CPU utilization values per site — revealing which sites consistently absorb new jobs under already-heavy CPU load?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS jobs_started, MIN(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.site_cpu_util') AS REAL)) AS min_site_cpu_util, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.site_cpu_util') AS REAL)) AS avg_site_cpu_util, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.site_cpu_util') AS REAL)) AS max_site_cpu_util FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Started' GROUP BY site ORDER BY avg_site_cpu_util DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Site-Level CPU Utilization at Job Execution Start

All four sites reached **100% CPU utilization** (max = 1.0) at the moment at least one job began executing, meaning every site has accepted new work while fully saturated at some point.

### Ranked by Average CPU Load (highest → lowest)

| Site | Jobs Started | Min Util | Avg Util | Max Util |
|------|-------------|----------|----------|----------|
| **UKDF** | 126 | 2.1% | **77.5%** | 100% |
| **Base** | 544 | 2.5% | **76.9%** | 100% |
| FrDF | 206 | 0.8% | 66.6% | 100% |
| USDF | 624 | 0.2% | 60.8% | 100% |

### Key Observations

- **UKDF and Base are the heaviest-loaded sites** at job start time, averaging ~77% CPU utilization — meaning jobs there routinely begin execution in an already-congested environment.
- **USDF absorbs the most jobs** (624 starts) but does so at a lower average load (60.8%), suggesting it has more headroom or scales capacity more effectively.
- **FrDF** sits in the middle at 66.6% average, with the lowest minimum across all sites (0.8%), indicating more variable load patterns.
- The **low minimums across all sites** (all under 3%) confirm that each site does occasionally accept jobs under near-idle conditions — but the high averages for UKDF and Base show those cases are the exception, not the rule.

**Operational implication:** UKDF and Base are the strongest candidates for CPU-related job queuing or slowdowns, as they consistently start new jobs when their CPUs are already heavily loaded.

## Inbound Network Pressure by Destination Site

Four destination sites received inbound transfers. Here is a summary ordered by average link load (highest to lowest), with link loads converted to GB/s and total bytes to GB:

| Site | Transfers | Avg Link Load | Max Link Load | Total Received |
|------|-----------|--------------|--------------|----------------|
| **Base** | 601 | 10.95 GB/s | 12.50 GB/s | 49.3 GB |
| **USDF** | 597 | 7.04 GB/s | 12.50 GB/s | 59.2 GB |
| **FrDF** | 2,953 | 1.21 GB/s | 1.25 GB/s | 271.3 GB |
| **UKDF** | 1,273 | 1.14 GB/s | 1.25 GB/s | 117.3 GB |

### Key Observations

- **Base faces the heaviest inbound pressure** by average link load (10.95 GB/s), reaching a peak of 12.50 GB/s — indicating its link was nearly fully saturated for much of the time transfers completed. This is despite receiving the *fewest* bytes (49.3 GB), suggesting a narrow-bandwidth link that is chronically stressed.

### Operational Implication
Base and USDF are the sites most at risk of inbound network bottlenecks; their links are saturating even at modest transfer volumes. FrDF absorbs the bulk of grid data movement but does so across a lower-capacity, less-stressed link.

messages.content:
## Jobs Most Throttled by Data Staging

Every one of the top 20 finished job executions shows a **transfer-queue percentage of exactly 100%** — meaning their entire queue wait was consumed by file transfer staging, with zero time spent waiting for compute resources.

### Key Findings

- **All 20 jobs ran at the "Base" site**, suggesting this site is a consistent bottleneck for data staging.
- **File transfer queue times range from ~1.57 to ~1.78 seconds**, with the lowest being job 1187 (1.5665 s) and the highest being job 1355 (1.7815 s).
- Because `file_transfer_queue_time = total_queue_time` in every row, **no resource waiting time contributed to queuing at all** for these jobs — staging was the sole source of delay.

### Interpretation

These jobs were not waiting for CPU slots; they were waiting exclusively for input data to be staged in. This pattern — 100% staging-driven queue time across 20 jobs all at the same site — points to a **systemic data locality or network bandwidth constraint at the Base site** rather than isolated incidents. Prioritizing data pre-placement or increasing staging throughput at Base would directly reduce the queue time for this entire class of jobs.

messages.content:
## Queue Time Breakdown by Site: Hardware vs. Data Bottlenecks

Across 4 sites and 1,500 finished job executions, the fraction of queue time attributable to resource waiting (hardware contention) versus the remainder (file transfer staging / data availability) varies dramatically.

---

### Site-by-Site Results

| Site | Jobs | Avg Resource Wait (s) | Avg Total Queue (s) | Resource-Wait % | Primary Bottleneck |
|------|------|-----------------------|---------------------|-----------------|--------------------|
| **USDF** | 624 | 0.144 | 0.137 | **105.02%** | Hardware contention ⚠️ |
| **Base** | 544 | 0.888 | 2.610 | **34.01%** | Mixed, data-leaning |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 10.876 | 52.067 | **20.89%** | Data availability |
| **FrDF** | 206 | 8.731 | 139.226 | **6.27%** | Data availability |

---

### Key Observations

1. **USDF is hardware-contention bottlenecked** — resource waiting (0.144 s) actually *exceeds* total queue time (0.137 s), producing an anomalous 105.02%. This likely reflects a timing/accounting edge case, but the signal is clear: virtually all queue delay at USDF is CPU/slot waiting, with negligible staging overhead. Queue times are also very short overall.

2. **FrDF is overwhelmingly data-bottlenecked** — at only 6.27% resource-wait, roughly **93.7%** of its average 139.2-second queue time is consumed by file transfer staging. FrDF has by far the longest total queue time of any site.

3. **UKDF is similarly data-bottlenecked** — 20.89% resource-wait against a 52.1-second average total queue means ~79% is staging delay, despite having the fewest jobs (126).

## Execution Duration by Retry Count — Base Site (Results Truncated at 200 Rows)

| 39 | 1 | **4.02 × 10⁻⁷** | same | same |
| 305–317 | 1 each | ~6.2–1.1 × 10⁻⁷ range | — | — |

1. **No simple "more retries = longer duration" pattern.** Jobs with retries 1–5 and 13–83 show average durations *slightly lower* than zero-retry jobs (avg 9.81 × 10⁻⁸). High retry counts in the 305–317 range also show short durations (~6–11 × 10⁻⁸).

For each source site in completed file transfers, what is the total bytes sent, average bandwidth, and number of outbound transfers — identifying which sites act as the heaviest data exporters on the grid?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.source_site') AS source_site, COUNT(*) AS transfer_count, SUM(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS FLOAT)) AS total_bytes_sent, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.bandwidth') AS FLOAT)) AS avg_bandwidth, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.bandwidth') AS FLOAT)) AS max_bandwidth FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileTransfer' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY source_site ORDER BY total_bytes_sent DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## File Transfer Export Summary by Source Site

Three sites act as data exporters across all completed file transfers:

| Source Site | Outbound Transfers | Total Bytes Sent | Avg Bandwidth | Max Bandwidth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **USDF** | 4,108 | 377.4 GB | 1.50 GB/s | 12.5 GB/s |
| **Base** | 704 | 71.2 GB | 9.70 GB/s | 12.5 GB/s |
| **Summit** | 612 | 48.6 GB | 11.89 GB/s | 12.5 GB/s |

### Key Findings

- **USDF is the dominant data exporter by a wide margin** — it sent 377.4 GB across 4,108 transfers, which is roughly **5.3× more data than Base and 7.8× more than Summit**. Its sheer transfer volume drives the grid's outbound data traffic.

- **USDF has the lowest average bandwidth (1.50 GB/s)**, far below Base (9.70 GB/s) and Summit (11.89 GB/s). This suggests USDF's transfers are often congested or contend heavily for link capacity given its outsized volume.

- **Summit and Base export far less total data** but operate near peak link efficiency — Summit's 11.89 GB/s average approaches the 12.5 GB/s maximum observed across all three sites.

- All three sites share the same maximum bandwidth (12.5 GB/s), indicating they connect to the same class of network links, but USDF's high concurrency pulls its average down significantly.

**Operational takeaway:** USDF warrants the closest attention for network capacity planning, as it drives the overwhelming majority of outbound data volume despite operating at a fraction of its theoretical peak bandwidth.

messages.content:
## Site-Level CPU Utilization at Job Execution Completion

Four sites are recorded. All share the same floor (minimum = **0.0**) and ceiling (maximum ≈ **1.0**), meaning every site has seen both fully idle and near-fully saturated conditions at the moment a job finished. The meaningful differentiator is the **average**, which reveals typical operating load:

| Site | Jobs Completed | Avg CPU Util | Max CPU Util |
|------|---------------|-------------|-------------|
| **Base** | 544 | **0.765** | 0.997 |
| **UKDF** | 126 | **0.761** | 0.997 |
| **FrDF** | 206 | **0.660** | 0.999 |
| **USDF** | 624 | **0.605** | 0.998 |

### Operational Takeaways

- **Consistently heavy (limited headroom):** **Base** and **UKDF** run at ~76% average CPU utilization — the highest of the four sites. Despite their near-zero minimums (idle bursts do occur), their averages indicate these sites routinely operate under significant load. They are the most at-risk of saturation-driven queuing delays.

- **Moderate load with more headroom:** **FrDF** averages ~66%, placing it in a middle tier with a reasonable ~34% headroom on average.

- **Most headroom:** **USDF**, despite completing the largest job count (624), averages only ~61% CPU utilization — the lowest of all sites — suggesting it is the most capacity-elastic or least loaded site in typical operation, despite occasionally peaking near full saturation like the others.

The universal minimum of 0.0 across all sites confirms that idle windows exist everywhere; the question of "saturation risk" is therefore determined primarily by the **average**, not the extremes.

## FileRead vs. FileWrite Duration by Site

A ratio **below 1.0** means reads finish faster than writes (read-optimised); a ratio **above 1.0** means writes finish faster than reads (write-optimised).

### Key Observations

- **FrDF and UKDF are strongly read-optimised.** Reads complete roughly 6–8× faster than writes at these sites. FrDF has the highest read throughput (2,953 read ops) and the fastest average read at 0.0094 s.

- **Base is mildly write-optimised** (ratio 1.44), with a relatively balanced workload (644 reads, 856 writes) and moderate durations on both sides.

### Operational Takeaway

FrDF and UKDF are well-suited for read-heavy workloads but show slower write throughput, which matters if output-writing jobs are scheduled there.

| **Base** | 544 | 1.20 | **−0.954** | −1.000 | −0.125 |
| **USDF** | 624 | 4.89 | −0.294 | −1.000 | −0.125 |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 5.16 | −0.287 | −1.000 | −0.125 |
| **FrDF** | 206 | 5.84 | −0.253 | −1.000 | −0.125 |

### Key Observations

- **Base** has by far the most negative avg cost/core (−0.954), running almost entirely single-core jobs (avg 1.20 cores). It also has the most jobs (544).
- **FrDF** has the least negative avg cost/core (−0.253) but the highest avg core count (5.84), suggesting heavier parallel workloads yield a proportionally smaller per-core cost signal.

messages.content:
## Per-Site I/O Read Fraction of Job Wall-Clock Duration

### Key Finding: I/O Read Time Exceeds Wall-Clock Duration at All Sites

A critical observation: the computed ratio (total_io_read_time ÷ duration) is **far greater than 1.0 at every site**, meaning `total_io_read_time` is systematically larger than `duration`. This indicates `total_io_read_time` likely represents **aggregated I/O time across multiple parallel reads or cores**, not a simple fraction of wall-clock time. The values should be interpreted as a multiplier, not a percentage.

---

### Results by Site (ordered by avg I/O ratio, descending)

| Site | Jobs | Avg I/O Ratio | Max I/O Ratio | Jobs w/ Non-Zero I/O |
|------|------|--------------|--------------|----------------------|
| **Base** | 544 | 2,133,237.8× | 6,520,385.0× | 544 (100%) |
| **USDF** | 624 | 1,679,290.8× | 17,681,287.4× | 624 (100%) |
| **FrDF** | 206 | 81,546.3× | 235,633.9× | 206 (100%) |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 77,377.4× | 300,432.6× | 126 (100%) |

---

### Operational Conclusions

1. **100% of finished jobs at every site report non-zero I/O read time** — disk I/O is universally present, not an edge case.
2. **Base and USDF are the most I/O-intensive sites** by a large margin (~20–27× higher ratios than FrDF/UKDF), with USDF having the single worst-case job (ratio of 17,681,287×).
3. **UKDF and FrDF are comparatively lighter on I/O**, with ratios roughly 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than Base/USDF.
4. Given the extreme ratios, **Base and USDF are the clear disk I/O bottleneck sites** and are the priority targets for storage optimization or caching interventions.

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk') AS disk, COUNT(*) AS write_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)) AS avg_effective_write_bw, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_write_bw') AS REAL)) AS avg_reported_write_bw, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)) / NULLIF(AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_write_bw') AS REAL)), 0) AS efficiency_ratio FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileWrite' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site, disk ORDER BY efficiency_ratio ASC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Disk Write Efficiency Analysis: All Sites Fall Well Below Hardware Specs

Across all 4 site/disk combinations, no site achieves even 50% of its rated disk write bandwidth. Here is the breakdown, ordered from worst to best efficiency:

| Site | Disk | Writes | Avg Effective BW | Avg Rated BW | Efficiency |
|------|------|--------|-----------------|--------------|------------|
| Base | BASE_DISK | 856 | 0.89 GB/s | 5.0 GB/s | **17.8%** |
| USDF | USDF_DISK | 1,199 | 3.35 GB/s | 10.0 GB/s | **33.5%** |
| UKDF | UKDF_DISK | 255 | 4.83 GB/s | 10.0 GB/s | **48.3%** |
| FrDF | FrDF_DISK | 408 | 4.98 GB/s | 10.0 GB/s | **49.8%** |

### Key Findings

- **Base is the most severe underperformer**: its effective write throughput (0.89 GB/s) is only **17.8%** of its rated 5.0 GB/s — despite having the *lower* hardware rating of all sites. It also accounts for 856 operations, making this a high-volume problem.
- **USDF** processes the most writes (1,199) but only reaches **33.5%** of its 10.0 GB/s spec (3.35 GB/s actual).
- **UKDF and FrDF** are the closest to spec but still cap out at **48.3%** and **49.8%** respectively — meaning even the best-performing sites waste roughly half their rated disk write capacity.
- The three sites rated at 10.0 GB/s show a clear progression (USDF → UKDF → FrDF), suggesting differences in contention, file sizes, or workload mix rather than hardware capability.

### Operational Implication
Write performance is *systematically* constrained across the entire grid — likely by concurrent I/O contention, small file overhead, or filesystem latency. Base warrants priority investigation given both the lowest absolute throughput and the worst efficiency ratio.

## Findings: Cost and Duration by Retry Count

### Cost — No Differentiation Whatsoever
Every retry group, without exception, has an **avg_cost of exactly –1.0**. Total cost is simply –1.0 × job count per group (e.g., –920.0 for the zero-retry group, –4.0 for the four-job groups, etc.). |---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 920 | 8.21 × 10⁻⁷ | 5.90 × 10⁻⁶ |

| 18 | 4 | 6.75 × 10⁻⁸ | 8.34 × 10⁻⁸ |

The data does **not** support the hypothesis that more retries systematically produce greater cost or longer wall-clock time. For questions about simulated grid behavior, you query the CGSim simulation database (an append-only EVENTS table) using the query_simulation_db tool, then explain the results in clear operational terms.

For each destination site, what is the count of completed inbound file transfers, the count of completed job executions, and the ratio of transfers to jobs — revealing on average how many file staging operations each job requires per site and which sites have the heaviest per-job data staging burden?

arguments.sql: SELECT site, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'FileTransfer' THEN cnt ELSE 0 END) AS inbound_transfer_count, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'JobExecution' THEN cnt ELSE 0 END) AS job_execution_count, CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'FileTransfer' THEN cnt ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'JobExecution' THEN cnt ELSE 0 END), 0) AS transfers_per_job FROM (SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.destination_site') AS site, 'FileTransfer' AS event_type, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileTransfer' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site UNION ALL SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, 'JobExecution' AS event_type, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site) GROUP BY site ORDER BY transfers_per_job DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Per-Site File Staging Burden

Four destination sites appear in the results, with dramatically different data-staging demands per job:

| Site | Inbound Transfers | Job Executions | Transfers per Job |
|------|:-----------------:|:--------------:|:-----------------:|
| FrDF | 2,953 | 206 | **14.3** |
| UKDF | 1,273 | 126 | **10.1** |
| Base | 601 | 544 | **1.1** |
| USDF | 597 | 624 | **1.0** |

### Key Observations

1. **FrDF carries the heaviest per-job staging burden** — each of its 206 completed jobs required an average of **14.3 inbound file transfers**, the highest ratio in the grid.

2. **UKDF is similarly transfer-intensive** — 10.1 transfers per job across 126 executions, suggesting these two European sites rely heavily on remote data staging rather than local data.

3. **Base and USDF are near-parity (≈1:1)** — with ratios of 1.1 and 1.0 respectively, jobs at these sites require roughly one file transfer each, implying most data is already local or the jobs are not data-staging-bound.

4. **Volume context**: FrDF and UKDF together account for 4,226 inbound transfers (2,953 + 1,273) but only 332 jobs, while Base and USDF handle nearly equal transfer and job counts (1,198 transfers, 1,168 jobs).

### Operational Implication
FrDF and UKDF are the primary candidates for data caching or pre-staging optimizations — reducing their ~10–14 transfers-per-job ratio would have the largest impact on staging overhead across the grid.

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS job_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_total_queue_time, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS avg_exec_duration, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)) AS avg_queue_to_exec_ratio, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)) AS max_queue_to_exec_ratio FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site ORDER BY avg_queue_to_exec_ratio DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Queue-to-Execution Ratio Analysis by Site

All four sites show **extreme queue pressure**: average queue-to-execution ratios range from tens of millions to over 135 million, meaning jobs spend orders of magnitude more time waiting than actually computing. This is driven by execution durations that are effectively near-zero (on the order of 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁷ simulation time units) against queue times measured in tens to hundreds of seconds.

### Site Rankings (by average ratio, worst to best)

| Site | Jobs | Avg Queue Time (s) | Avg Exec Duration | Avg Q/Exec Ratio | Max Q/Exec Ratio |
|------|------|--------------------|-------------------|------------------|-----------------|
| **FrDF** | 206 | 139.23 | 1.53 × 10⁻⁶ | **135,899,199** | **593,650,763** |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 52.07 | 1.26 × 10⁻⁶ | **84,803,437** | **378,907,292** |
| **Base** | 544 | 2.61 | 1.18 × 10⁻⁷ | **30,728,035** | **72,799,793** |
| **USDF** | 624 | 0.14 | 1.03 × 10⁻⁶ | **13,327,216** | **115,170,423** |

### Key Observations

- **FrDF is the most pressured site** — its average queue time of 139.23 s is nearly 3× that of UKDF (52.07 s) and ~1,000× that of USDF (0.14 s), yielding the highest average ratio of ~135.9 M and a peak ratio of ~593.7 M.
- **UKDF** follows with an average ratio of ~84.8 M and a max of ~378.9 M across only 126 jobs, suggesting concentrated but severe congestion.
- **USDF**, despite having the largest job count (624), has the lowest average ratio (~13.3 M) and the smallest average queue time (0.14 s), making it the most efficiently scheduled site — though its max ratio of ~115.2 M indicates occasional severe spikes.
- **Base** sits in the middle on average (~30.7 M) but has the smallest execution durations (1.18 × 10⁻⁷), amplifying the ratio even though its queue time (2.61 s) is low.

### Operational Implication
FrDF and UKDF require immediate attention to scheduling and/or input staging pipelines — their absolute queue times (~139 s and ~52 s respectively) confirm real waiting, not just a ratio artifact. USDF's low average queue time indicates its scheduler is handling load well despite the highest job volume.

## Compute Throughput by Site (Finished Job Executions)

Across **4 sites** and **1,500 total finished jobs**, compute throughput (flops ÷ duration) varies dramatically by site.

### Site Rankings (Average Throughput)

| Site | Jobs | Avg (GFlops/s) | Min (GFlops/s) | Max (GFlops/s) |
|------|------|----------------|----------------|----------------|
| **FrDF** | 206 | **18.69** | 3.20 | 25.60 |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 16.51 | 3.20 | 25.60 |
| **USDF** | 624 | 15.65 | 3.20 | 25.60 |
| **Base** | 544 | **3.83** | 3.20 | 25.60 |

### Key Observations

- **FrDF is the top performer** at an average of ~18.69 GFlops/s, despite running only 206 jobs — the second-lowest workload volume.
- **UKDF and USDF are competitive**, at ~16.51 and ~15.65 GFlops/s respectively, though USDF carries the heaviest job load (624 jobs).
- **Base is a significant underperformer** — its average of ~3.83 GFlops/s is roughly **4–5× lower** than the other three sites, despite handling 544 jobs (second-highest volume). This is a clear bottleneck.

### Operational Takeaway
Base requires investigation: it is absorbing a high job volume while consistently delivering low throughput. FrDF, though lightly loaded, is the most efficient site and may be underutilized.

## Finished FileWrite Workload by Site and Disk

Four site/disk combinations are active, all using a single dedicated disk per site. Results below use **MB** throughout (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes), rounded to the nearest whole MB.

| Site | Disk | Write Count | Total Written | Avg File Size | Max File Size |
|------|------|------------:|-------------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| USDF | USDF_DISK | 1,199 | 267,492 MB | 223 MB | 2,445 MB |
| FrDF | FrDF_DISK | 408 | 132,557 MB | 325 MB | 2,431 MB |
| UKDF | UKDF_DISK | 255 | 59,590 MB | 234 MB | 2,150 MB |
| Base | BASE_DISK | 856 | 45,156 MB | 53 MB | 2,022 MB |

### Key Observations

- **Heaviest total write workload: USDF_DISK** — absorbs 267,492 MB across 1,199 operations, more than double the next busiest disk and accounting for the majority of all bytes written across the grid.
- **Highest write frequency: USDF_DISK** at 1,199 writes, followed by Base (856), FrDF (408), and UKDF (255).
- **Largest individual files: USDF_DISK** hosts the single largest write at 2,445 MB. All four disks handle files in the ~2 GB range, suggesting a consistent upper file-size ceiling across the grid.
- **Highest average file size: FrDF_DISK** at 325 MB per file — notably larger than USDF (223 MB) and UKDF (234 MB), meaning FrDF handles fewer but proportionally larger writes.
- **BASE_DISK is an outlier on average size** — despite 856 writes (second highest volume), its average file size is only 53 MB, indicating it predominantly handles many small files rather than large ones.

For each job that has both a completed allocation and a started execution, what is the average, minimum, and maximum time gap (execution start TIME minus allocation finish TIME) per site — exposing how long jobs idle between being placed on a site and actually beginning to compute, signalling slow handoff pipelines?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(alloc.METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS job_count, AVG(exec_start.TIME - alloc.TIME) AS avg_gap, MIN(exec_start.TIME - alloc.TIME) AS min_gap, MAX(exec_start.TIME - alloc.TIME) AS max_gap FROM EVENTS alloc JOIN EVENTS exec_start ON alloc.JOB_ID = exec_start.JOB_ID AND exec_start.EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND exec_start.STATE = 'Started' WHERE alloc.EVENT = 'JobAllocation' AND alloc.STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site ORDER BY avg_gap DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Job Idle Time Between Allocation and Execution Start, by Site

The analysis covers 4 sites and reveals very large differences in how quickly jobs transition from placement to actual computation.

| Site | Jobs | Avg Gap (s) | Min Gap (s) | Max Gap (s) |
|------|------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| **FrDF** | 206 | **130.63** | 7.69 | 227.79 |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 41.29 | 10.47 | 92.19 |
| **USDF** | 624 | 3.54 | 0.03 | 10.60 |
| **Base** | 544 | 1.90 | 0.02 | 8.25 |

### Key Findings

- **FrDF is by far the slowest handoff site.** Its average idle gap of **130.63 seconds** is more than **3× worse than UKDF** (41.29 s) and nearly **70× worse than Base** (1.90 s). The worst single job at FrDF waited **227.79 seconds** — nearly 4 minutes doing nothing after being allocated.

- **UKDF is a secondary concern**, with an average of 41.29 s and a maximum of 92.19 s. Its gap is non-trivial but far smaller than FrDF's.

- **USDF and Base are healthy**, with average gaps of 3.54 s and 1.90 s respectively, and maximum gaps under 11 seconds. These sites represent normal handoff behavior.

### Operational Recommendation
FrDF and UKDF should be investigated for slow post-allocation pipelines — likely causes include delayed pilot framework signaling, slow staging checks, or resource contention in job launch daemons. FrDF in particular shows a **consistently high floor** (minimum gap of 7.69 s) suggesting a systematic delay, not just occasional spikes.

For finished file transfers, what is the total bytes sent outbound, total bytes received inbound, net byte difference, and outbound-to-inbound ratio per site — categorising each site as a net data importer or exporter and quantifying the degree of asymmetry in the grid's data flow?

arguments.sql: SELECT site, SUM(outbound_bytes) AS total_bytes_sent, SUM(inbound_bytes) AS total_bytes_received, SUM(outbound_bytes) - SUM(inbound_bytes) AS net_bytes, CASE WHEN SUM(inbound_bytes) > 0 THEN ROUND(CAST(SUM(outbound_bytes) AS REAL) / SUM(inbound_bytes), 4) ELSE NULL END AS outbound_to_inbound_ratio FROM (SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.source_site') AS site, CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) AS outbound_bytes, 0.0 AS inbound_bytes FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileTransfer' AND STATE = 'Finished' UNION ALL SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.destination_site') AS site, 0.0 AS outbound_bytes, CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) AS inbound_bytes FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileTransfer' AND STATE = 'Finished') GROUP BY site ORDER BY net_bytes DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Data Flow Asymmetry Across the Grid (Finished File Transfers)

Five sites participate in file transfers. They split cleanly into **net exporters** (positive net bytes) and **net importers** (negative net bytes).

---

### Net Exporters — more data sent out than received

| Site | Bytes Sent | Bytes Received | Net Outbound | Outbound/Inbound Ratio |
|------|-----------|----------------|--------------|------------------------|
| **USDF** | 377,397,339,392 | 59,203,409,927 | +318,193,929,465 | **6.3746×** |
| **Summit** | 48,570,203,040 | 0 | +48,570,203,040 | — (no inbound) |
| **Base** | 71,221,399,051 | 49,347,520,166 | +21,873,878,885 | **1.4433×** |

- **USDF** is by far the dominant exporter, sending roughly 6.37 bytes for every 1 it receives — the highest asymmetry of any bidirectional site.
- **Summit** sends exclusively; it received zero bytes, making it a pure one-way data source.
- **Base** is a mild exporter, with a ratio just above 1.44×.

---

### Net Importers — more data received than sent

| Site | Bytes Sent | Bytes Received | Net Inbound | Outbound/Inbound Ratio |
|------|-----------|----------------|-------------|------------------------|
| **FrDF** | 0 | 271,307,216,585 | −271,307,216,585 | 0.0 (pure import) |
| **UKDF** | 0 | 117,330,794,805 | −117,330,794,805 | 0.0 (pure import) |

- Both **FrDF** and **UKDF** are purely passive receivers — zero bytes sent outbound.
- **FrDF** absorbs the largest inbound volume of any single site (271,307,216,585 bytes).

---

### Key Takeaways

1. **USDF + Summit + Base are the grid's data sources**; USDF alone accounts for the vast majority of outbound traffic.
2. **FrDF + UKDF are pure sinks**, receiving all their data from elsewhere and contributing nothing outbound — a ratio of exactly 0.0 for both.
3. The grid exhibits **strong directional asymmetry**: data flows predominantly from USDF toward the European facilities (FrDF, UKDF), with Base and Summit as secondary sources.

For finished FileRead operations grouped by site and host, what are the average, minimum, and maximum reported disk_read_bw values and the bandwidth range (max minus min) — identifying hosts whose read bandwidth fluctuates most widely, suggesting storage contention or inconsistent hardware behaviour?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, json_extract(METADATA, '$.host') AS host, COUNT(*) AS read_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_read_bw') AS REAL)) AS avg_disk_read_bw, MIN(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_read_bw') AS REAL)) AS min_disk_read_bw, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_read_bw') AS REAL)) AS max_disk_read_bw, MAX(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_read_bw') AS REAL)) - MIN(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.disk_read_bw') AS REAL)) AS bw_range FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileRead' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site, host HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY bw_range DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Disk Read Bandwidth Fluctuation Analysis

### Key Finding: Zero Fluctuation Across All Observed Hosts

Despite the query ordering results by bandwidth range (highest first), **every single host in the returned results shows a `bw_range` of exactly 0.0** — meaning no bandwidth fluctuation whatsoever was observed on any host.

### Bandwidth by Site (Consistent, Flat Values)

| Site | Disk Read Bandwidth (avg/min/max) | Bandwidth Range | Hosts Visible |
|------|----------------------------------|-----------------|---------------|
| **Base** | 5,000,000,000 B/s (5 GB/s) | 0.0 | 10 (cpu-0 through cpu-9) |
| **FrDF** | 10,000,000,000 B/s (10 GB/s) | 0.0 | 15 (cpu-0 through cpu-21, partial) |

### Notable Details
- The full result set contains **112 host/site combinations** (results truncated at 25 shown).
- Read counts per host vary considerably — e.g., FrDF_cpu-0 handled **155 reads** while FrDF_cpu-16 handled only **45** — yet bandwidth remains perfectly flat regardless of load.
- **No host shows storage contention or inconsistent hardware behaviour** based on bandwidth fluctuation. The disk read bandwidth appears to be a fixed, configured value per site rather than a dynamically measured one, making it unsuitable for contention detection in this simulation dataset.

messages.content: You are AskPanDA, an expert assistant for ATLAS Grid computing and PanDA workload management. For questions about simulated grid behavior, you query the CGSim simulation database (an append-only EVENTS table) using the query_simulation_db tool, then explain the results in clear operational terms.

For finished job executions, what is the count of completed jobs, average duration, average cost, and total cost per host within each site — identifying the busiest and most expensive individual compute nodes across the grid?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, json_extract(METADATA, '$.host') AS host, COUNT(*) AS job_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS avg_duration, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cost') AS REAL)) AS avg_cost, SUM(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.cost') AS REAL)) AS total_cost FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site, host ORDER BY job_count DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Finished Job Executions: Per-Host Summary

**Dataset scope:** 112 unique site–host combinations (results truncated at 25 rows shown here).

---

### Busiest Compute Nodes (by job count)

The **Base** site completely dominates the top 10, accounting for all highest-volume hosts:

| Rank | Host | Site | Jobs | Avg Duration (s) |
|------|------|------|------|-----------------|
| 1 | Base_cpu-1 | Base | 61 | 9.59e-08 |
| 2 | Base_cpu-2 | Base | 60 | 1.33e-07 |
| 3 | Base_cpu-9 | Base | 58 | 9.93e-08 |
| 4 | Base_cpu-5 | Base | 56 | 9.22e-08 |
| 5 | Base_cpu-0 | Base | 54 | 8.80e-08 |

Outside Base, the busiest single node is **UKDF_cpu-0** at 22 jobs.

---

### Cost Data — Uniform Sentinel Value
Every host reports an average cost of **−1.0** and a total cost equal to **−1 × job_count** (e.g., Base_cpu-1 = −61.0, Base_cpu-2 = −60.0). This uniform −1.0 per job indicates the cost field is unpopulated or is a placeholder in this simulation run — **no meaningful cost differentiation exists across nodes**.

---

### Duration Pattern by Site
Base hosts run jobs in the **sub-100 nanosecond** range (e.g., 8.8e-08 s), while remote sites are roughly 4–15× slower: USDF nodes average ~3.8e-07 to ~1.4e-06 s, and the single visible FrDF node (FrDF_cpu-27) has the longest average at **1.25e-06 s** across 14 jobs. This reflects Base's role as the high-speed local cluster.

---

### Key Takeaway
**Base_cpu-1 is the busiest node** (61 jobs), and the entire Base site handles far more jobs per host than any remote site. Cost ranking mirrors job count exactly due to the −1.0 sentinel, so no true cost differentiation can be drawn from this simulation output.

messages.content: You are AskPanDA, an expert assistant for ATLAS Grid computing and PanDA workload management. For questions about simulated grid behavior, you query the CGSim simulation database (an append-only EVENTS table) using the query_simulation_db tool, then explain the results in clear operational terms.

For completed file transfers, how do average transfer duration, average file size, and average effective throughput vary across link-load congestion buckets (low < 0.3, medium 0.3–0.7, high > 0.7) — revealing whether higher network congestion systematically degrades transfer performance?

arguments.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.link_load') AS REAL) < 0.3 THEN 'low' WHEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.link_load') AS REAL) < 0.7 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'high' END AS link_load_bucket, COUNT(*) AS transfer_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS avg_duration, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL)) AS avg_file_size_bytes, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL), 0)) AS avg_throughput_bps FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'FileTransfer' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY link_load_bucket ORDER BY link_load_bucket LIMIT 200

messages.content: {"columns": ["link_load_bucket", "transfer_count", "avg_duration", "avg_file_size_bytes", "avg_throughput_bps"], "rows": [["high", 5424, 98.69159132267211, 91664627.8545354, 7679912.881403499]], "row_count": 1}

## File Transfer Performance by Link-Load Congestion Bucket

### Key Finding: Only One Congestion Tier Observed

All **5,424 completed file transfers** fall exclusively in the **high congestion bucket** (link load > 0.7). There are **zero transfers** in the low (< 0.3) or medium (0.3–0.7) buckets. Because only a single bucket is populated, a cross-bucket comparison of congestion effects is not possible from this dataset.

### High-Congestion Bucket Summary

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Transfer count | 5,424 |
| Average duration | 98.7 seconds |
| Average file size | ~91.7 MB |
| Average effective throughput | ~7.68 MB/s |

### Operational Takeaways

- **The network operates persistently under high load.** Every single completed transfer occurred when the link load exceeded 0.7, suggesting the simulated grid links are chronically congested rather than occasionally saturated.
- **Performance at high congestion:** Transfers of ~91.7 MB files take roughly 99 seconds on average, yielding ~7.68 MB/s. Whether this is "degraded" relative to uncongested conditions cannot be determined from this data alone — there are no low- or medium-load transfers to benchmark against.
- **No congestion gradient is visible** in these results. Any investigation into whether higher congestion *systematically* degrades performance would require simulation runs that produce transfers across all three load tiers.

## Grid-Wide CPU Utilization at Job Execution Completions

### Overall Picture
The simulation produced **only one hour-bucket (bucket 0, covering the first hour)**, meaning all job completions occurred within that single interval. There is no temporal spread to compare across buckets.

### Bucket 0 Detail

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Hour bucket | 0 (0–3,600 s) |
| Completed jobs | **1,500** |
| Min grid_cpu_util | **0.0** |
| Avg grid_cpu_util | **~2.80 × 10⁻¹³** |
| Max grid_cpu_util | **~4.36 × 10⁻¹³** |

### Key Observations

1. **All 1,500 job completions are compressed into the first hour.** There are no later buckets, so no temporal trend in CPU utilization can be drawn from this simulation run.

2. **Grid CPU utilization is effectively zero across every completing job.** All three statistics (min, avg, max) are at or indistinguishably close to zero (values on the order of 10⁻¹³). This signals that, at the moments these jobs finish, the grid as a whole is carrying negligible computational load relative to its total capacity.

3. **No periods of peak or trough pressure are detectable.** With utilization essentially zero throughout and all events in a single bucket, there is no variation to expose. This likely reflects either an extremely large grid capacity relative to the 1,500-job workload, or that the utilization metric is recorded near an idle baseline at completion time.

**Operational takeaway:** The simulation does not enter a CPU-stressed regime at any point during job completions; the grid remains idle relative to its capacity for the entire run.

messages.content:
## Finished Job Execution Profile by Site

All four sites run processors at the same speed: **3.2 GFlops/s**. The differences lie in job volume, flops intensity, and core usage.

| Site | Jobs | Avg Flops/Job | Avg Cores | Total Flops |
|------|------|--------------|-----------|-------------|
| **USDF** | 624 | 22,860 | 4.89 | 14,264,934 |
| **FrDF** | 206 | 36,709 | 5.84 | 7,561,971 |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 28,904 | 5.16 | 3,641,949 |
| **Base** | 544 | 946 | 1.20 | 514,731 |

### Key Observations

- **USDF** dominates in raw compute volume, accounting for 14.26 M total flops — nearly double FrDF — driven by the highest job count (624 jobs), despite a moderate per-job flops load.
- **FrDF** runs the most computationally intensive jobs on average (36,709 flops/job) and uses the most cores per job (5.84), yet its lower job count (206) places it second overall.
- **UKDF** has the fewest jobs (126) but mid-range intensity (28,904 flops/job, 5.16 cores), yielding the smallest contribution among the three data federation sites (3.64 M total flops).
- **Base** is a clear outlier: despite 544 jobs (second highest volume), its per-job workload is tiny — only **946 flops/job** on average with just 1.20 cores — producing a negligible total of 514,731 flops. This site appears to handle lightweight or coordination tasks rather than heavy compute.

messages.content:
## FileRead Performance by Site and Size Bucket

**No large (>1 GB) reads appear in the results** — all activity falls into the small (<100 MB) and medium (100 MB–1 GB) buckets only.

---

### Summary Table

| Site | Bucket | Read Count | Avg Disk BW | Avg Duration (s) | Avg File Size (MB) |
|------|--------|-----------|-------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Base | small | 576 | 5 GB/s | 0.1631 | 79.5 |
| Base | medium | 68 | 5 GB/s | 0.0777 | 115.2 |
| FrDF | small | 1,825 | 10 GB/s | 0.00770 | 76.1 |
| FrDF | medium | 1,128 | 10 GB/s | 0.01216 | 117.4 |
| UKDF | small | 794 | 10 GB/s | 0.00788 | 76.6 |
| UKDF | medium | 479 | 10 GB/s | 0.01294 | 117.9 |
| USDF | small | 3,352 | 10 GB/s | 0.3516 | 76.4 |
| USDF | medium | 2,108 | 10 GB/s | 0.4902 | 117.3 |

---

### Key Operational Findings

1. **Two-tier bandwidth configuration:** Base runs at **5 GB/s** disk read bandwidth; FrDF, UKDF, and USDF all run at **10 GB/s** — consistent across both size buckets within each site.

2. **Duration scales with file size at FrDF, UKDF, and USDF** (as expected): medium files (~117 MB) take roughly 1.5–1.6× longer than small files (~76 MB), consistent with proportional size differences at fixed bandwidth.

3. **Base is anomalous:** Medium files (avg 115 MB) actually read *faster* (0.0777 s) than small files (avg 79.5 MB, 0.1631 s), despite identical 5 GB/s bandwidth. This likely reflects disk contention or I/O scheduling effects under the much higher volume of small reads (576 vs. 68).

4. **USDF has the slowest absolute durations** despite 10 GB/s bandwidth — 0.35 s for small and 0.49 s for medium — roughly 45× slower than FrDF/UKDF at the same bandwidth, suggesting persistent disk contention given its dominant read volume (5,460 total reads vs. ≤2,953 elsewhere).

5. **No evidence of sequential throughput gains for larger files** across sites — bandwidth is fixed by configuration, and duration increases proportionally with size rather than improving efficiency.

messages.content:
## Inbound File Transfer Bandwidth Utilisation by Destination Site

All four receiving sites show extremely poor exploitation of their available link capacity — none exceeds **0.35%** average utilisation.

| Site | Transfers | Avg Effective Throughput | Avg Reported Bandwidth | Avg Util. Ratio | Min Util. Ratio |
|------|-----------|--------------------------|------------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| **FrDF** | 2,953 | 0.91 MB/s | 1,250 MB/s | **0.073%** | 0.037% |
| **USDF** | 597 | 16.43 MB/s | 12,500 MB/s | **0.131%** | 0.115% |
| **UKDF** | 1,273 | 2.33 MB/s | 1,250 MB/s | **0.186%** | 0.118% |
| **Base** | 601 | 43.58 MB/s | 12,500 MB/s | **0.349%** | 0.117% |

### Key Findings

- **FrDF is the worst offender** — by far the busiest site (2,953 transfers) yet averaging only 0.91 MB/s against a 1,250 MB/s link, yielding an average utilisation of just 0.073% and dropping as low as 0.037% in the worst individual transfer. High transfer volume is clearly not translating into efficient use of the link.

- **USDF and Base** share the same 12,500 MB/s reported bandwidth. Base achieves roughly 2.7× better average utilisation (0.349% vs. 0.131%) despite similar transfer counts (~601 vs. 597), suggesting Base jobs carry larger or faster-completing files.

- **Minimum utilisation ratios cluster around 0.11–0.12%** for USDF, UKDF, and Base, while FrDF's minimum (0.037%) is an outlier indicating occasional near-idle transfers.

- The universal sub-0.35% utilisation across all sites points to a systemic issue — likely many small/short transfers, high latency overhead, or queue serialisation — rather than a single site misconfiguration.

messages.content:
## Job Allocation Completion: Storage Utilisation by Site

All four sites show **extremely low storage utilisation** at allocation completion — no site is remotely close to saturation. Here is the breakdown:

| Site | Allocations | Avg Site Storage Util | Max Site Storage Util | Avg Grid Storage Util | Max Grid Storage Util |
|------|-------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| **Base** | 544 | 0.0423% | 0.0600% | 0.0126% | 0.0145% |
| **USDF** | 624 | 0.0165% | 0.0168% | 0.0116% | 0.0118% |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 0.0007% | 0.0068% | 0.0138% | 0.0177% |
| **FrDF** | 206 | 0.0002% | 0.0021% | 0.0127% | 0.0193% |

*(Utilisation ratios multiplied by 100 to express as percentages.)*

### Key Findings

- **Base** is the most site-storage-loaded site, with the highest average (0.0423%) and peak (0.0600%) site storage utilisation at allocation completion — roughly **3× higher** than USDF and orders of magnitude higher than UKDF and FrDF.
- **USDF** has the most allocations (624) yet very consistent site storage load (avg ≈ max ≈ 0.0165–0.0168%), suggesting steady, predictable usage.
- **UKDF** and **FrDF** have negligible site-level storage load (<0.007% peak).
- **Grid-level storage utilisation** is broadly consistent across all sites (0.012%–0.019% max), indicating no grid-wide bottleneck.

### Operational Conclusion
**No site shows storage saturation.** Even Base — the highest-loaded — peaks at only ~0.06% site storage utilisation. The scheduler is not placing jobs onto storage-constrained infrastructure; storage is a non-issue in this simulation run.

messages.content:
## Job Execution Analysis by Site and Core Count

### Coverage
The results span **12 site × core-count combinations** across 4 sites (Base, FrDF, UKDF, USDF) and 3 core configurations (1, 4, 8 cores). Total job counts per site: Base 544, USDF 624, FrDF 206, UKDF 126. USDF is the busiest site; Base is second. At Base and USDF, 1-core jobs dominate; at FrDF and UKDF, 8-core jobs dominate.

---

### Duration Scaling (Parallelism vs. Speed)
Duration consistently **increases** with core count across all sites, indicating that higher-core jobs carry heavier workloads — not that more cores slow execution. Durations are in simulation time units:

| Site | 1-core avg | 4-core avg | 8-core avg | 1→4 ratio | 1→8 ratio |
|------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Base | 8.37e-8 | 4.37e-7 | 3.99e-6 | ~5.2× | ~47.7× |
| FrDF | 8.10e-8 | 4.59e-7 | 2.54e-6 | ~5.7× | ~31.4× |
| UKDF | 8.32e-8 | 4.67e-7 | 2.70e-6 | ~5.6× | ~32.5× |
| USDF | 8.30e-8 | 4.38e-7 | 2.51e-6 | ~5.3× | ~30.2× |

The jump from 4→8 cores is notably steeper at Base (~9× longer) versus USDF and FrDF (~5–6×), suggesting Base's 8-core jobs are disproportionately heavier. Maximum durations show high variability at 8 cores (e.g., FrDF max 7.87e-6 vs. avg 2.54e-6), indicating outlier-heavy 8-core workloads.

---

### Cost and Cost-Per-Core
**All cost values are −1.0** across every site and core count — a sentinel indicating cost was not recorded in this simulation run. Consequently, the avg_cost_per_core figures (−1.0, −0.25, −0.125) are purely arithmetic artefacts of dividing −1 by the core count, not meaningful efficiency metrics. **No cost-efficiency conclusions can be drawn from this dataset.**

---

### Key Takeaways
1. **No diminishing-returns signal is detectable** from duration alone; longer 8-core durations reflect heavier jobs, not parallelism inefficiency.
2. **USDF runs the most 4-core and 8-core jobs** (366 and 190 respectively), making it the primary high-parallelism site.
3. **Cost data is absent** (−1.0 universally); cost-per-core analysis requires a simulation run that populates the cost field.

messages.content:
## Network Performance by Inter-Site Transfer Route

The query covers **10 distinct source→destination routes** across 4 sites (Summit, Base, USDF, FrDF, UKDF).

---

### Volume and Traffic Dominance

The top two routes account for the vast majority of data movement:
- **USDF→FrDF**: 2,845 transfers, **260.7 GB** total — by far the highest-volume corridor
- **USDF→UKDF**: 1,173 transfers, **107.7 GB** total
- All remaining 8 routes each moved under 54 GB, with the lowest being **Summit→UKDF** at 1.15 GB across only 14 transfers

---

### Two Distinct Bandwidth Tiers

Routes split cleanly into two classes based on reported bandwidth:
- **High-capacity links (12.5 GB/s reported):** Base↔USDF, Summit→Base, Summit→USDF — these are internal/near-site connections with very low latency (as low as 0.001 s for Summit→Base)
- **Standard WAN links (1.25 GB/s reported):** All routes involving FrDF or UKDF — these carry intercontinental traffic with higher latency (0.12–0.216 s)

---

### Most and Least Efficient Corridors (Effective Throughput)

| Route | Avg Effective Throughput | Avg Latency |
|---|---|---|
| **Summit→Base** *(most efficient)* | **~48.4 MB/s** | 0.001 s |
| Base→USDF | ~16.5 MB/s | 0.095 s |
| USDF→Base | ~16.4 MB/s | 0.095 s |
| Summit→USDF | ~15.9 MB/s | 0.096 s |
| Base→FrDF | ~10.0 MB/s | 0.160 s |
| Summit→FrDF | ~9.5 MB/s | 0.161 s |

messages.content:
## FileWrite Performance by Site and Storage Utilization Bucket

### Key Finding Up Front: No Storage Saturation Observed

**All 2,718 finished FileWrite operations fall exclusively in the "low" storage utilization bucket (< 0.3).** There are zero writes recorded under medium or high storage utilization. Consequently, the original question — whether high saturation degrades write performance — **cannot be answered from this dataset**; there is no contrasting data.

---

### Per-Site Summary (all "low" utilization bucket)

| Site | Write Count | Avg Effective Throughput | Avg Reported Disk Write BW | Avg Duration |
|------|------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|--------------|
| Base | 856 | 0.89 GB/s | 5.00 GB/s | 0.107 s |
| FrDF | 408 | 4.98 GB/s | 10.00 GB/s | 0.075 s |
| UKDF | 255 | 4.83 GB/s | 10.00 GB/s | 0.057 s |
| USDF | 1,199 | 3.35 GB/s | 10.00 GB/s | 0.149 s |

*(Throughput values converted from B/s to GB/s for readability; underlying values from results.)*

---

### Notable Observations

1. **Base is an outlier**: Its reported disk bandwidth is 5.00 GB/s (half of the other sites), and its effective throughput of 0.89 GB/s is roughly **18% of its rated bandwidth** — a much larger gap than the other sites.
2. **FrDF and UKDF are most efficient**: Effective throughput reaches ~4.83–4.98 GB/s against a 10 GB/s rated BW (~48–50% utilization).
3. **USDF has the most writes (1,199)** and the longest average duration (0.149 s), yet still achieves 3.35 GB/s effective throughput (~33% of rated BW).
4. **The saturation question is unanswerable here**: Without medium or high utilization data, no comparison across buckets is possible.

For finished job executions grouped by site and retry bucket (zero retries versus one or more retries), what are the job count, average file_transfer_queue_time, average resource_waiting_queue_time, and average total_queue_time — revealing whether jobs that require retries systematically experience longer pre-execution staging delays than first-attempt jobs?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, CASE WHEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.retries') AS INTEGER) = 0 THEN 'no_retries' ELSE 'one_or_more_retries' END AS retry_bucket, COUNT(*) AS job_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.file_transfer_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_file_transfer_queue_time, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.resource_waiting_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_resource_waiting_queue_time, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.total_queue_time') AS REAL)) AS avg_total_queue_time FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site, retry_bucket ORDER BY site, retry_bucket LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Retry Impact on Pre-Execution Queue Delays — by Site

### The Core Pattern
Across all four sites, **first-attempt jobs (no retries) have a resource_waiting_queue_time of exactly 0.0**, while **retried jobs always carry a non-zero resource_waiting component**. The extra total queue burden on retried jobs is entirely driven by this resource-waiting penalty, not by longer file-transfer staging.

---

### Site-by-Site Breakdown

| Site | Retry Bucket | Jobs | Avg File Transfer Queue | Avg Resource Waiting | Avg Total Queue |
|------|-------------|------|------------------------|---------------------|-----------------|
| Base | no_retries | 284 | 2.04 | 0.00 | 2.04 |
| Base | one_or_more_retries | 260 | 1.38 | 1.86 | 3.23 |
| FrDF | no_retries | 165 | 131.02 | 0.00 | 131.02 |
| FrDF | one_or_more_retries | 41 | 128.40 | 43.87 | 172.27 |
| UKDF | no_retries | 74 | 46.33 | 0.00 | 46.33 |
| UKDF | one_or_more_retries | 52 | 33.88 | 26.35 | 60.23 |
| USDF | no_retries | 397 | −0.08 | 0.00 | −0.08 |
| USDF | one_or_more_retries | 227 | 0.13 | 0.40 | 0.52 |

---

### Key Findings

1. **Resource waiting is the discriminating factor.** No first-attempt job at any site waits for resources (0.00 in every case). Retried jobs incur resource-waiting delays of 1.86 (Base), 43.87 (FrDF), 26.35 (UKDF), and 0.40 (USDF).

2. **File-transfer queue time does NOT explain the gap.** Retried jobs actually show *lower* file-transfer queue times than first-attempt jobs at Base (1.38 vs. 2.04), FrDF (128.40 vs. 131.02), and UKDF (33.88 vs. 46.33). Only USDF shows a minor increase (0.13 vs. −0.08, the latter likely a simulation artifact).

3. **FrDF is the most adversely affected site.** Retried jobs accumulate an average total queue time of 172.27 versus 131.02 for first-attempt jobs — a difference of ~41 time units, almost entirely from resource waiting.

4. **USDF is nearly unaffected.** Queue times are negligible in both buckets, suggesting abundant or well-matched resources at that site.

### Conclusion
Retried jobs *do* experience systematically longer total pre-execution delays, but the root cause is **resource contention** (resource_waiting_queue_time), not file-staging bottlenecks. File transfer queuing is comparable or even slightly better for retried jobs, ruling out network/storage as the retry driver.

3. **Short simulation window:** All 5,424 transfers were initiated and resolved within a single hour, suggesting either a compact simulation run or that the workload completes very quickly relative to the 1-hour bucketing resolution. Finer time buckets (e.g., 5-minute intervals) would be needed to expose intra-hour congestion bursts.

messages.content:
## Pre-Execution Queue Time Breakdown by Site

Across all four sites, **data staging (file transfer queue time) dominates over compute contention (resource waiting queue time)** at most locations, but the balance shifts significantly by site.

---

### Site-by-Site Summary

| Site | Jobs | Avg Total Queue (s) | FT Queue Fraction | RW Queue Fraction | Dominant Factor |
|------|------|--------------------|--------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| **FrDF** | 206 | 139.23 | **93.7%** | 6.3% | Data staging |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 52.07 | **79.1%** | 20.9% | Data staging |
| **Base** | 544 | 2.61 | **66.0%** | 34.0% | Data staging |
| **USDF** | 624 | 0.14 | ~0% (−5.0%) | ~105% | Compute contention |

---

### Key Observations

1. **FrDF has the longest absolute queue delays** (139.23 s average), almost entirely driven by data staging — file transfer wait accounts for 93.7% of total queue time. Compute contention is negligible there (6.3%).

2. **UKDF** follows the same pattern at a lower magnitude (52.07 s total), with staging still dominant at 79.1% but compute contention more visible at 20.9%.

3. **Base** has very low total queue time (2.61 s) but maintains the staging-dominant pattern (66.0% vs. 34.0%).

4. **USDF is the outlier**: total queue time is near-zero (0.14 s), and the file transfer fraction is effectively zero (−5.0%, a floating-point artifact of near-zero values). Resource waiting accounts for the entirety (~105%) of what little queue time exists — meaning **USDF jobs face compute contention, not data staging delays**, though the absolute delays are trivial.

**Operational takeaway**: FrDF and UKDF are the sites where reducing data staging latency (pre-staging, caching, network bandwidth) would have the greatest impact on pre-execution delays. USDF is not a concern at current load levels.

messages.content:
## FileRead Hotspot Analysis

### Key Finding: No Repeated Reads

The most critical result is that **every file in the top 20 has a read_count of exactly 1**, each read at exactly **1 distinct site**. There are no "hot" files being read multiple times — disk activity is spread uniformly across unique files, with no single asset dominating through repetition.

### Uniform Disk Performance

All 20 files share an identical `avg_disk_read_bw` of **10,000,000,000 bytes/s (10 GB/s)**, indicating reads are hitting a consistently fast storage tier across the grid with no variation in disk throughput.

### File Size and Duration Range

All files are LSST SingleFrame calibration FITS files. Sizes span from **74,650,662 bytes** (`lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_977_0000.fits`) to **131,541,729 bytes** (`lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_982_0000.fits`). Given the 10 GB/s bandwidth, read durations are extremely short — most fall between **~0.0075 and ~0.013 seconds**.

One notable outlier: `lsst_SingleFrame_Cal_982_0001.fits` has a disproportionately high `avg_read_duration` of **0.0327 seconds** despite its 109,154,821-byte size, which is not the largest file — suggesting possible transient disk contention at that moment.

### Operational Conclusion

There are **no grid-wide disk hotspots** in this simulation snapshot. Every file is read exactly once at one site, meaning disk I/O load is fully distributed. The workload exhibits a pure single-pass read pattern — no caching benefit opportunity exists from repeated access, and no file represents a disproportionate load burden.

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(*) AS job_count, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.flops') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.speed') AS REAL), 0)) AS avg_expected_compute_s, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) AS avg_actual_duration, AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.duration') AS REAL)) / NULLIF(AVG(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.flops') AS REAL) / NULLIF(CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.speed') AS REAL), 0)), 0) AS overhead_multiplier FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' AND STATE = 'Finished' GROUP BY site ORDER BY overhead_multiplier DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Compute Time: Expected vs. Actual by Site

All four sites show a striking result: **actual job durations are substantially shorter than the raw expected compute time** (flops ÷ speed), producing overhead multipliers well below 1.0. This likely reflects multi-core parallelism — the speed metric appears to represent single-core throughput, while jobs run across multiple cores, finishing faster than the single-threaded estimate.

| Site | Jobs | Avg Expected Compute (s) | Avg Actual Duration (s) | Overhead Multiplier |
|------|------|--------------------------|--------------------------|---------------------|
| **Base** | 544 | 2.96 × 10⁻⁷ | 1.18 × 10⁻⁷ | **0.400** |
| **USDF** | 624 | 7.14 × 10⁻⁶ | 1.03 × 10⁻⁶ | **0.144** |
| **UKDF** | 126 | 9.03 × 10⁻⁶ | 1.26 × 10⁻⁶ | **0.139** |
| **FrDF** | 206 | 1.15 × 10⁻⁵ | 1.53 × 10⁻⁶ | **0.133** |

### Key Observations

- **Base** has the **highest multiplier (0.40)** — its actual duration is 40% of the single-core compute estimate, meaning the least parallelism gain (or the most residual overhead relative to expected time). It also has the smallest absolute expected compute times, suggesting shorter, lighter jobs.
- **FrDF** has the **lowest multiplier (0.133)**, with actual duration only 13% of expected compute time — the greatest apparent parallelism benefit or the most aggressive multi-core use.
- **USDF and UKDF** sit closely together at 0.144 and 0.139 respectively, indicating similar execution characteristics.
- In absolute terms, **FrDF jobs are the most compute-intensive** (avg expected: 1.15 × 10⁻⁵ s), followed by UKDF, USDF, and Base — yet all finish well under their single-threaded estimate.

**Bottom line:** No site shows a multiplier > 1 (no site where scheduling/I/O inflates duration beyond raw compute). Base is the site where actual runtime is proportionally *closest* to the raw compute estimate, making it the candidate most worth examining for scheduling or I/O overhead in relative terms.

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, json_extract(METADATA, '$.host') AS host, SUM(CASE WHEN EVENT = 'FileRead' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS read_count, SUM(CASE WHEN EVENT = 'FileWrite' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS write_count, SUM(CASE WHEN EVENT = 'FileRead' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) ELSE 0 END) AS total_bytes_read, SUM(CASE WHEN EVENT = 'FileWrite' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) ELSE 0 END) AS total_bytes_written, SUM(CASE WHEN EVENT = 'FileRead' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN EVENT = 'FileWrite' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.size') AS REAL) ELSE 0 END), 0) AS read_write_byte_ratio FROM EVENTS WHERE STATE = 'Finished' AND EVENT IN ('FileRead', 'FileWrite') GROUP BY site, host ORDER BY (read_count + write_count) DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Disk I/O Profile by Site and Host

The query covers 112 host-level rows across four sites (Base, FrDF, UKDF, USDF); the 25 rows shown here represent the busiest nodes by total operation count.

---

### Top I/O-Intensive Nodes (by total disk operations)

| Host | Site | Reads | Writes | Total Ops | Bytes Read (GB) | Bytes Written (GB) | R/W Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UKDF_cpu-8 | UKDF | 157 | 18 | **175** | 15.95 | 8.33 | 1.91 |
| FrDF_cpu-0 | FrDF | 155 | 16 | **171** | 15.55 | 8.16 | 1.91 |
| USDF_cpu-26 | USDF | 145 | 26 | **171** | 13.16 | 6.61 | 1.99 |
| FrDF_cpu-22 | FrDF | 153 | 9 | **162** | 14.56 | 7.02 | 2.07 |
| USDF_cpu-19 | USDF | 137 | 22 | **159** | 11.74 | 5.58 | 2.11 |

*(Bytes converted from raw values in results: divided by 1,000,000,000)*

---

### Key Findings

**Every visible node is read-heavy** — all 25 shown rows have a read/write byte ratio > 1.0. No write-dominant host appears in this dataset.

**FrDF, UKDF, and USDF are strongly read-skewed**, with ratios ranging from ~1.83 (USDF_cpu-3) up to **2.14 (FrDF_cpu-24)**. This suggests these remote data-facility nodes are predominantly consuming pre-staged input files.

**Base site nodes are the most balanced**, with ratios between 1.08 (Base_cpu-3 at 1.079, Base_cpu-2 at 1.09) and 1.46 (Base_cpu-8 at 1.46). Base_cpu-2 and Base_cpu-9 come closest to parity, and notably Base_cpu-2 has *more writes than reads* by count (69 reads vs. 96 writes), though bytes read still slightly exceed bytes written (ratio 1.09).

**Most bytes read overall**: UKDF_cpu-8 at 15.95 GB, followed by FrDF_cpu-0 at 15.55 GB and FrDF_cpu-22 at 14.56 GB.

**Most bytes written overall**: UKDF_cpu-8 at 8.33 GB, followed by FrDF_cpu-0 at 8.16 GB and USDF_cpu-3 at 7.32 GB.

---

### Summary

The workload is universally read-dominated. Non-Base sites run near a **2:1 read/write byte ratio**, consistent with a pattern of reading large input datasets and writing smaller output files. Base site nodes moderate this toward **~1.1–1.5**, suggesting they handle more output-intensive or intermediate processing tasks.

For questions about simulated grid behavior, you query the CGSim simulation database (an append-only EVENTS table) using the query_simulation_db tool, then explain the results in clear operational terms.

For each site, what is the average grid_cpu_util recorded at JobExecution Started events versus Finished events, and the difference between them — revealing whether grid-wide CPU pressure typically rises or falls over a job's lifetime and which sites most often complete work into an increasingly saturated grid?

arguments.sql: SELECT json_extract(METADATA, '$.site') AS site, COUNT(CASE WHEN STATE = 'Started' THEN 1 END) AS started_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN STATE = 'Finished' THEN 1 END) AS finished_count, AVG(CASE WHEN STATE = 'Started' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.grid_cpu_util') AS REAL) END) AS avg_grid_cpu_util_at_start, AVG(CASE WHEN STATE = 'Finished' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.grid_cpu_util') AS REAL) END) AS avg_grid_cpu_util_at_finish, AVG(CASE WHEN STATE = 'Finished' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.grid_cpu_util') AS REAL) END) - AVG(CASE WHEN STATE = 'Started' THEN CAST(json_extract(METADATA, '$.grid_cpu_util') AS REAL) END) AS util_delta FROM EVENTS WHERE EVENT = 'JobExecution' GROUP BY site ORDER BY util_delta DESC LIMIT 200

messages.content:
## Grid CPU Utilisation: Started vs. Finished, by Site

### Key Findings

All four sites show **negative util_delta**, meaning grid-wide CPU utilisation is marginally *lower* at the moment jobs finish than when they started. No site completes work into an increasingly saturated grid — the pattern runs uniformly in the opposite direction.

| Site | Jobs (Started/Finished) | Avg grid_cpu_util @ Start | Avg grid_cpu_util @ Finish | Delta (Finish − Start) |
|------|------------------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|
| **Base** | 544 / 544 | 3.304 × 10⁻¹³ | 3.302 × 10⁻¹³ | −1.46 × 10⁻¹⁶ |
| **USDF** | 624 / 624 | 3.264 × 10⁻¹³ | 3.258 × 10⁻¹³ | −5.96 × 10⁻¹⁶ |
| **UKDF** | 126 / 126 | 1.463 × 10⁻¹³ | 1.456 × 10⁻¹³ | −6.28 × 10⁻¹⁶ |
| **FrDF** | 206 / 206 | 9.402 × 10⁻¹⁴ | 9.331 × 10⁻¹⁴ | −7.11 × 10⁻¹⁶ |

### Operational Interpretation

1. **All deltas are negative and vanishingly small** — the recorded `grid_cpu_util` values are themselves near-zero (order 10⁻¹³–10⁻¹⁴), indicating the simulated grid is running at near-idle CPU utilisation throughout.

2. **Ranking by most pressure change:** FrDF shows the largest absolute drop (−7.11 × 10⁻¹⁶), followed by UKDF (−6.28 × 10⁻¹⁶) and USDF (−5.96 × 10⁻¹⁶). Base is the most stable (−1.46 × 10⁻¹⁶).

3. **No site completes jobs into a more-loaded grid.** The slight universal decline suggests that, on average, jobs finish as the grid is marginally *releasing* CPU pressure — consistent with jobs freeing resources as they complete.

4. **USDF handles the most jobs** (624) while Base is close behind (544); UKDF processes the fewest (126). The per-job CPU signal is too small to draw meaningful operational distinctions across sites.

For finished job executions per site, what is the first-attempt success rate (fraction with retries = 0), the average retries among jobs that did retry (retries > 0), and the maximum retries observed — revealing which sites have the most reliable job execution pipelines and which suffer chronic failure-and-retry cycles?

messages.content:
## Job Execution Reliability by Site

Four sites are covered across 1,500 finished job executions in total. Results are sorted from least to most reliable by first-attempt success rate.

| Site | Total Jobs | First-Attempt Success Rate | Avg Retries (retried jobs only) | Max Retries |
|------|-----------|---------------------------|----------------------------------|-------------|
| Base | 544 | 52.2% | 366.5 | 607 |
| UKDF | 126 | 58.7% | 1,258.3 | 1,307 |
| USDF | 624 | 63.6% | 97.0 | 188 |
| FrDF | 206 | 80.1% | 1,245.5 | 1,371 |

### Key Observations

**Most reliable pipeline — FrDF**: 80.1% of jobs succeed on the first attempt. However, the jobs that *do* retry average 1,245.5 retries and top out at 1,371 — suggesting a hard binary outcome: jobs either sail through or spiral into extreme retry loops.

**Most resilient to retry storms — USDF**: While its 63.6% first-attempt rate is middling, its retrying jobs average only 97 retries (max 188). This is by far the most bounded retry behavior, indicating failures are transient and recover quickly.

**Worst chronic failure site — UKDF**: Only 58.7% first-attempt success, and retrying jobs average 1,258 retries (max 1,307). Nearly half of all jobs hit a severe failure cycle.

**Base**: The lowest first-attempt success rate at 52.2%, meaning nearly half of its 544 jobs require retries. Retrying jobs average 366.5 retries (max 607) — serious but less extreme than UKDF/FrDF.

### Operational Takeaway
USDF offers the most operationally predictable behavior. Base requires immediate attention due to volume (most jobs) combined with low reliability. UKDF and FrDF exhibit a dangerous bimodal pattern — jobs that fail at all tend to fail catastrophically, warranting investigation into what triggers those failure spirals.

messages.content:
## FileWrite Performance Under Grid Storage Saturation

### Key Finding: No High-Saturation Conditions Observed

Across all 4 sites, **grid storage utilization never came close to the 0.8 threshold**. The maximum observed `grid_storage_util` values were:

| Site | Total Writes | Max grid_storage_util | High-Saturation Writes | Avg Duration (Normal) |
|------|-------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------|
| USDF | 1,199 | 0.000167 | 0 | 0.1489 s |
| Base | 856 | 0.000168 | 0 | 0.1071 s |
| FrDF | 408 | 0.000237 | 0 | 0.0746 s |
| UKDF | 255 | 0.000192 | 0 | 0.0568 s |

### Interpretation

- **Zero high-saturation writes** were recorded at any site — the > 0.8 threshold was never breached. Peak utilization topped out at just **0.000237** (FrDF), roughly **3,370× below** the saturation threshold.
- Because no writes occurred under high-saturation conditions, the high-saturation average duration is **undefined (null)** everywhere — there is simply no comparison to make.
- Under normal conditions, write durations range from **0.0568 s (UKDF)** to **0.1489 s (USDF)**, reflecting differences in file size or disk throughput across sites, not storage saturation effects.

### Conclusion

This simulation shows **no evidence that grid-level storage saturation degrades write performance**, because grid storage saturation never materialized. The grid operated at a tiny fraction of its storage capacity throughout the entire run.
